utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in these proceedings. Your Honours, yesterday we left off at the point when we were commenting on the Prosecutor's brief, the parts that have to do with the alleged contradictions between the statements made by Miroslav Tadic and the statements made by Radovan Antic, Jovo Savic, Stevan Nikolic, and Simo Zaric. The Defence believes that there is no contradiction whatsoever. If one looks at pages 16778 and 16779, when Witness Antic testified and he says that Miroslav Tadic telephoned to the command on the 17th of April in the morning and asked whether his presence was absolutely indispensable and Witness Antic said to him that it wasn't. Furthermore, he confirmed the assignment that Miroslav Tadic had. All of it starting from the 18th of April, 1992 onwards. So there is no contradiction in view of what Miroslav Tadic had stated. Simo Zaric on page 19254 says that on the 18th of April, Commander Antic issued orders to collect illegal weapons in the 4th quarter, and that both he and Tadic were informed about it on that day. Goran Buzakovic was another witness in the Defence case and he was a direct participant in the arms collection in the 4th quarter. The Prosecutor takes his testimony out of context, and he suggests to the witness that Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric had the task of overseeing arms collection. However, he keeps silent with regard to the answers given by Witness Buzakovic. On page 16672, he says that on that day, and on the previous day, he did not see Miroslav Tadic in the places where he was involved in collecting weapons. As for the date when he started collecting weapons, he refers to the 18th of April. The Defence furthermore does not see any contradiction whatsoever that the Prosecutor refers to, and this has to do with the testimony of Miroslav Tadic and the testimony of Witness Nikolic, especially not in the part that the Prosecutor quoted, that is, D47/4, paragraphs 36 and 37. Furthermore, in their final brief, the Prosecution invokes the statements of Witness C who allegedly saw Miroslav Tadic on the 17th of April, early in the morning, in his street, as he was walking in front of a tank. The testimony of Witness C is in contradiction to all other statements. First of all, no tank appeared in Bosanski Samac in that street on the early -- in the early morning of the 17th. That morning, Witness C was not at his home, which was after all confirmed by Stojan Damjanovic in his statement on page 17784, when he described the meeting with the father of Witness C, who was concerned about his son, who had not appeared at home that day. If the Trial Chamber wants to know where Witness C was that morning, they should just look at D25/4 and there on the list there you will find his name. It is quite clear where he was that morning, like most Prosecution witnesses who testified here. In the same street, a few houses away from Witness C's house, were Osman Jasarevic and Delic Dragan, Prosecution witnesses who lived there. None of them, although they were asked, had seen either a tank or Miroslav Tadic walking along the street in front of this alleged tank. On the contrary; as opposed to the Prosecution, the Defence believes that the testimonies of Simo Zaric, Stevan Nikolic, Radovan Antic, Jovo Savic, testified to the fact that Miroslav Tadic had a minor role in the 4th Detachment and that he made no contribution whatsoever to the takeover of power. Furthermore, the Prosecution claims that there was coordination between the 4th Detachment and the paramilitaries. This is incorrect, because the Defence proved during its case that the weapons handover was a voluntary exercise. No houses were entered. There was no coercion whatsoever. No lists were compiled of persons who had had weapons, and therefore people were not arrested on that basis or rather on those grounds. The Defence believes that it was proven during these proceedings that people were arrested on the basis of lists that had been found at the police station because it is evident that many arrests took place subsequently, after these lists had been found, and therefore the grounds for arrest were membership in the paramilitary unit that was organised by the SDA. This is as far as the town of Bosanski Samac is concerned at least. Witnesses Goran Buzakovic, Radovan Antic, Fadil Topcagic who took part in the weapons collection, just like all Prosecution witnesses who testified here, stated that no one was arrested on that occasion. Furthermore, the Prosecution says that it is irrelevant whether the 4th Detachment took part in the takeover of Samac during that night or whether they simply joined in this exercise on the 17th of April in the morning and that the effect of the intentional inactivity of the 4th Detachment with a view to power takeover and the activities of the 4th Detachment in terms of taking weapons away and going out to the embankment was the consolidation of power of the new Serb regime and in keeping with joint criminal enterprise with a view to persecution. The Defence believes that the Prosecution did not present a shred of evidence that would corroborate this thesis. The role of the 4th Detachment and how they understood their assignment was best described by Witness Marko Kuresevic, president of a party that Simo Zaric belonged to and most of his witnesses. Kuresevic was a serious and credible witness and he said that the role of the 4th Detachment was not to protect the authorities, either Serb, Croat, or some third authorities, but the protection of all inhabitants of Bosanski Samac, as well as the territory of the municipality. Marko Kuresevic said that he did take part in the war, as a member of the 4th Detachment, but not in order to remove the non-Serb population and to have the non-Serb population leave this territory. He said that he took part in this war in order to protect his family, to protect this territory, to protect his wife, who was a Croat, and his daughters-in-law who are Croats. You will find this on page 17870. That is the position of the Defence of Miroslav Tadic and the reason why he was engaged in the 4th Detachment. His awareness and action were aimed at helping all citizens through his activities, not acting with any kind of intention of expelling non-Serbs from this territory. Furthermore, when the Prosecutor speaks about the inactivity of the 4th Detachment, they refer to the statement made by Jovo Savic, when he gives his personal opinion that the members of the command were aware of the fact that the inactivity of the 4th Detachment made it possible for the new regime to come into power. However, his opinion does not have probative value in the opinion of the Defence because it is simply an opinion and this does not show that there is had a link between the takeover of the town and the activities of Miroslav Tadic. Jovo Tadic testified that he did not talk to a single member of the Crisis Staff or any members of the command about these developments. He said that he was presenting his personal opinion and his personal position. When cross-examined by the Defence of Blagoje Simic when explicitly asked about what he knew about the discrimination of the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac he said this was his opinion. He said this on page 17271. Furthermore, witness Jovo Savic presented his opinion about arrests on discriminatory grounds and he also presented his assumptions as he said to my colleague Mr. Pantelic when he was asked about that. And his response to a direct question put by the Prosecutor as to whether he had ever visited the buildings of the Territorial Defence, the SUP, the high school or places where detainees were held, he said he had never been there. I'm referring to 17154 and 17155. Furthermore, when the Prosecution asked him whether he was ever present during the interrogation of detainees or whether he ever visited military prisons, the witness gave a negative answer yet again. This is page 17156.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you are too fast. Could the please slow down so the interpreters can keep pace with you and also be able to interpret every word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour [Interpretation] Furthermore, when the Prosecutor asked witness Savic to described what happened in Samac and to speak about the roles of various authorities in Samac, witness Jovo Savic said that he was in Samac very seldom and that in that period, 1992 and 1993, he was primarily if he command in Pelagicevo and that he did not have any knowledge as to what had been going on in Samac and that primarily everything that he was saying is his very own opinion. This is 17169. Jovo Savic is a fact witness, not an expert. His personal opinion does not have probative value and the political position that he presents is also of no probative value. He is supposed to testify. His personal political views cannot serve as grounds for establishing knowledge of the fact that by failing to act, persecution was supported in Bosanski Samac. After all, the Prosecution did not put a single question to Miroslav Tadic as to whether this omission on the part of the 4th Detachment helped the establishment of the regime based on discriminatory grounds. It seems to us that the first time that they remembered that this was the case was in their final brief. And what was this position and power that Miroslav Tadic had so that through his omission and failure to act he could have contributed to anything let alone the establishment of a government on allegedly discriminatory grounds? Further on, when the Prosecution speaks about illegal arrests and the role of Miroslav Tadic, it gives sweeping statements without stating what his contribution to these arrests is. The Prosecutor says that there is ample evidence that the arrests took place on discriminatory basis. As opposed to that, there is evidence that arrests were carried out on the basis of lists found in the police station and related to unlawful armed formations of the SDA and HDZ, and that these persons were arrested for the fact that they were suspected of having committed crimes that are punishable in any legal system. The Defence has to comment on the double standards of the Prosecution. In paragraph 144, the Prosecutor, when speaking about the captured Serbs in Odzak, called them the Serb soldiers, the military prisoners. As for the arrested Muslims detained in Samac, the Prosecutor refers to them as imprisoned civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said arrested armed Muslims. So I'm talking about line 17 on page 7. Arrested armed Muslims. The Defence also proved that all the persons arrested that Dragan Delic referred to and that the Prosecutor refers to in paragraph 151 and who were with them at the time were members of the paramilitary unit of the SDA and the HDZ and they were members of the Territorial Defence of the BH, an armed formation as it was described by Alija Fitozovic and as it was represented in document D51/3. Or that there was a suspicion that they participated in the arming, which was the reason why Dragan Delic was arrested. The Defence never claimed that all persons arrested had taken part in armed operations. Most of them certainly did, like Ibrahim Salkic, the Dagovic brothers, Hasan Subasic, Kemal Mehinovic, Izet Izetbegovic, Witness N, Witness A, Witness M, Witness M, and many others. Which in the opinion of the Defence was proven through the testimony of many witnesses. The statement of Dragan Delic confirms a fact that is opposite to what the Prosecution has been claiming and that is that there is no link between the searches, the arms handover and the arrest, because Delic was arrested only towards the end of May 1992, when dubious financial transactions were revealed in the company where he was general manager. Witness Sarkanovic, that the Prosecutor refers to, is mention -- mentions only a few cases of arrest of persons who were not on lists. One of them is Hasan Izetbegovic, who was released after having given a statement and that is what Sarkanovic said. The Prosecution confirms what their own witnesses said, that people did not know why Witness M was arrested and that this was not explained, especially in view of Witness M. And this is in contrast to all the evidence presented, especially the evidence that was introduced in relation to his trial in Bijeljina, that is D24/3 and also the testimony of witness Arandzic, Stevan who was wounded by Witness M on the 17th of April. He testified through deposition 169, 170. The claim made by the Prosecution that people were arrested due to fabrications and bizarre criminal activity is totally groundless. Witness P himself that the Prosecutor refers to confirmed on page 11534 that he had been armed, that he had been commander of an illegal military unit in his own village. Are these fabricated allegations and bizarre criminal activities? What about Ibrahim Salkic, a member of a sabotage group as he testified himself on page 3182? Was he a leader of a group that offered armed resistance? And Hasan Subasic, a member of this same group. Are they innocent passers-by and persons who are arrested only because they were Muslims and Croats. Many witnesses, both of the Prosecution and of the Defence, saw them walking through town armed and in the military formation. Witness G said that she saw Hasan Subasic and he had purportedly been sitting at his own home. When witness G testified, that is something that very few people can forget, who ever heard it. Is it probable that she lied? The Prosecution in their brief say that the authorities under the control of Muslims in Sarajevo had abolished the crime of armed rebellion and that accusations that the Muslims had rebelled against their own state are groundless and incorrect because in the territory of Republika Srpska these regulations were in force and people like Witness M were tried and convicted for such crimes. If one looks at document D24/3, one will see that Witness M was tried and convicted on the grounds of armed rebellion, that particular crime. In their final brief, paragraph 156, the Prosecution claims that the policemen, the paramilitaries, coordinated the arrests in keeping with lists which could only have been compiled by the Crisis Staff. The Prosecutor does not offer a single proof for this allegation, nor do they refer to any particular document or testimony. What is the Prosecution basing this claim upon? The Defence does not seem to understand. Neither do we understand how they concluded that Stevan Todorovic was appointed chief by the Crisis Staff. During this trial, it has been proven beyond doubt that Stevan Todorovic was not appointed by the Crisis Staff. When the Prosecution speaks about the reasons for arrests of certain political officials of the HDZ, the only grounds given is persecution and they refer to Miroslav Tadic's testimony and a sentence in that testimony which has been taken out of the context. Forgetting conveniently to mention that when Miroslav Tadic said political prisoner, he meant prisoners who had been arrested. Political officials of the SDA and the HDZ were arrested because they headed an armed formation that killed 1.600 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On page 10, line 8, He meant politicians who had been arrested not prisoners who had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is page 10, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the correction. That is why it is important to be a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, when speaking about Zasavica and the arrests of people, the Prosecution claims that the people were transferred from Bosanski Samac to Zasavica in May, not a shred of evidence has been offered that in May or in June anyone was brought to Zasavica to be isolated, not a single witness from Tisina, as the Prosecutor claims, did not confirm that they were indeed in Zasavica. Witness Q described in his testimony that all the surrounding villages were abandoned by Croats prior to the outbreak of conflict. Witness P described, in his testimony, that people, that is, women and children who had been taken to Crkvina from Zasavica were eventually brought back to Zasavica but does not mention any of the inhabitants of the surroundings villages as being brought back to Zasavica. As far as the connection between the arrests of non-Serbs and the exchanges that took place, the Prosecution has not offered a single piece of evidence to confirm the nexus between those two occurrences. People were arrested for reasons that have been mentioned many times, but not because of the exchanges. Witness Stevan Todorovic, on page 9563, said clearly that only the police had the authorities to release or arrest a person before the procedure was taken over by the Prosecution. Miroslav Tadic has also been accused of cruel and inhumane treatment of non-Serb civilians. Again, the Prosecution in paragraphs 186 to 188 accuses Miroslav Tadic without offering proof or evidence and does not specify what exactly the cruel and inhumane treatment of non-Serb civilians entailed. Miroslav Tadic himself said in his testimony that when in July he heard that certain people entered the prison to beat prisoners there, he drew Stevan Todorovic's attention to that and Stevan Todorovic told him to mind his own business. As most of the citizens of Samac, Miroslav Tadic was simply afraid of Stevan Todorovic. When he spoke about the massacre in Crkvina, Miroslav Tadic said that certain things were not done precisely because of the fear that people had, fear of Stevan Todorovic and the Specials from Serbia. However, Miroslav Tadic expressed his willingness to find the bodies of those who had been killed in Crkvina to shed light on the crime and not to hush it up as the Prosecutor claims. Miroslav Tadic never ceased to work on that task to this very day as testified by witness Velimir Maslic on 14215. In his interview of 1998, Miroslav Tadic made no secret of his knowledge of that event, but he also spoke of the great fear that took hold of people following that particular event. In paragraph 202, the Prosecution ties Miroslav Tadic to cheating and keeping prisoners away, keeping prisoners hidden without a single proof by constructing a link between Simo Zaric, who was allegedly seen outside the TO building when he was visiting the International Red Cross and think this sufficient to have Miroslav Tadic convicted of holding prisoners in inhumane conditions. The link between the arrival of the International Committee of the Red Cross and Miroslav Tadic the Prosecution derives from an unfinished sentence in part of the interview by Stevan Todorovic. When presenting this part of the interview, the Prosecution -- of the Prosecution Stevan Todorovic did not provide any kind of answer which is -- and no wonder, regarding the part of the interview that the witness was shown which contains an unfinished sentence which in that form can be interpreted in several ways. Unlike -- as opposed to that, Velimir Maslic, who was a competent person, provided a detailed and repeated description of all the contacts with the International Committee of the Red Cross in Bosanski Samac. There is the part of the interview where Stevan Todorovic speaks who the representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the police, and the executive committee came to see but it wasn't Miroslav Tadic. The Prosecution finds this part of the interview inconvenient and that's why they did not confront Stevan Todorovic with that particular section of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but just as to clarify my own picture of what you are saying. On page 12, line 5, you say keeping prisoners hidden without a single proof by constructing a link between Simo Zaric, who was allegedly -- do you really mean Simo Zaric or should it be Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we heard testimony of a witness who saw during the visit of the International Red Cross Simo Zaric allegedly out the TO building, outside the SUP building, and the Prosecutor, in his final brief, claims that Zaric and Tadic worked together on hiding this without mentioning a single piece of evidence placing Tadic in this context and without explaining what their role -- what the role of Tadic was in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, the Prosecution claiming in paragraph 110 that the Crisis Staff made a decision to transfer prisoners to Batkovici does not offer a single testimony that the prisoners were transferred to the prison pursuant to a decision by Andrija Bilosevic. This was ascertained during this trial. However the Crisis Staff was not even in existence when this event took place. At any rate, the Defence of Miroslav Tadic believes that Miroslav Tadic had nothing whatsoever to do with holding civilians and detaining them in inhumane conditions. This is also true of Zasavica, because many witnesses confirmed that they were taken to Zasavica at the end of August and beginning of September 1992, when Miroslav Tadic had nothing whatsoever to do with the civilian authorities. Furthermore, the assertion that civilians were held in Zasavica for the exchanges has not been proved because Miroslav Tadic had nothing to do with Zasavica nor did he ever go to Zasavica, except once as described in his interview. And as testified by Witness K, witness for the Prosecution who claims that she never saw him in Zasavica. Furthermore some of those people went home and then went to be exchanged as testified by witness Gordana Pavlovic when speaking about Almira Bobic who was in Zasavica and then returned home in December 1993, only to exchanged later on. That was in depositions page 81. On the basis of everything that has been presented in this trial, the Defence believes that Miroslav Tadic is not responsible for these three counts of the indictment that he has been charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Lukic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I will move on and speak about count 3 of the indictment, inhumane conditions. I will talk about forced labour. The Defence has offered in their work, a detailed analysis of the concept of forced labour or, rather, work obligation. Right at the outset, I would like to point out that international enactments and documents fully define work obligation and when, according to the legislation of a certain country, this work obligation can be assigned. According to the Prosecution, their interpretation of forced labour follows from the fact that dangerous, illegal, humiliating and unpaid work was done. The Defence explained that any kind of work in town at that time was dangerous, in town or throughout the territory, in a state of war, so there were incidents of civilians getting killed when they were working in shops in the town centre. All work was legitimate, because it was envisaged by provisions and by laws. The Prosecution, in formally defining who was in charge of the work obligation, refers to two quotes by Djordje Tubakovic and Simo Zaric. However, if we analyse accurately all the testimonies, you can understand very clearly what these two witnesses were actually saying. I wonder how it was possible that in the Prosecutor's trial brief, in paragraph 225, footnote 561, that the Prosecutor found convenient the testimony of Djordje Tubakovic and only several days later here in this courtroom we heard this very witness giving oral evidence and the Prosecution finding the witness totally inconvenient and making an oral motion with the Court to reject his entire testimony. In paragraph 19 of Exhibit D184/3, which is Djordje Tubakovic's statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. That's not what I said. I'd object to that. That's misquoting counsel. If you want to check the record. I said that his testimony was not worthy of belief in relation to Mr. Tadic, in my argument. It wasn't that all of his testimony was not worthy of belief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Your Honours to correct myself in that respect, but later I will speak again about certain portions and how the Prosecution seemed to like one witness at one time and dislike the same witness at another time. Paragraph 19 of Exhibit D184/3, statement by Djordje Tubakovic, there is an accurate definition of who exactly was in charge of the work obligation which was the secretariat for National Defence. Not a single word of the witness in that paragraph brings Miroslav Tadic into any kind of even loose connection with work obligation as such. What the paragraphs states is the very essence of all the evidence and all the testimonies that clearly point to who was responsible and in charge of the work obligation. Simo Zaric, whom the Prosecutor also refers to their interview, Exhibit Number P141, claims, when speaking about work obligation, that it was physical labour and that the person in charge was Bozo Ninkovic on behalf of the secretariat for National Defence. In paragraph 226, the Prosecution mistakenly establishes that work had to be voluntary, and they construct a mistaken link or a false link as to the person really had a choice to work or not to work and they refer to the Krnojelac judgement, paragraph 471. However, in the Krnojelac judgement, where forced labour is referred to and when it is established whether the person really took up forced labour of their own free will and whether there was any choice at all, we're talking about an entirely different case. We are talking about persons who are going to forced labour from the prison in which they are held, persons to which the work obligation does not apply. Another set of regulations is applied to such persons in keeping with the rules of those prisons. Defence witness DW2/3 described how he volunteered to go and perform work while he was in detention. As a consequence of that, he had certain benefits in his status as detainee. Prosecution witnesses for Batkovic went to the same kind of voluntary labour as testified by Witness I in DW8/3. When the same witness, DW2/3, was released from detention he was released to the same company and to the same tasks that he had before. He was given a decision on work obligation and he returned to the job that he had throughout the period relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Witness I. If I remember correctly, there wasn't any Witness I before this Tribunal. Here it's on line 19 and 20. There is something that is not particularly clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On page 16, line 20, I was referring to Witness DW8/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see, yes. Not Witness I. Can we clear this? Because in line 20, page 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I had in mind. Instead of the word Witness I, it should read Witness DW8/3. So this thesis on the existence of voluntary choice for someone to choose whether they wished to work or not and trying to prove the existence of forced labour through that is mistaken and a parallel is drawn from a totally different situation. The procedural matters related to work obligation in this case is legal and regulated by the law and by the law on work obligation. It is not a voluntary action as the word itself says, and there can be punishment in case of non-compliance. Now, who is it that decides on work obligation? Witness K testified, and my colleague Pantelic referred to that yesterday in connection with the statement about the computer of the Crisis Staff. I will say that she did not see the signature on the invitation that was issued. We should point out that Witness Safet Dagovic and Ahmet Sehapovic confirmed that issued call-ups for work obligations were signed by Bozo Ninkovic. Bozo Ninkovic himself on page 1338 stated that lists were compiled by coordinators, by the coordinator of the work units and that at the beginning the coordination was Dzevad Kapetanovic, "Beg," the very same man that Witness K refers to. The Prosecution claims that the secretariat for People's Defence was formally responsible for forced labour and I would like to stress the word "formally" here. Nowhere is it explained why is that secretariat considered to be formally responsible when its competency and responsibility are regulated by law, decree, and there are many pieces of written evidence which go to show the relationship between all of the users of the work obligation and the department of the Ministry of Defence. This department, pursuant to all of the evidence and written documents, reported to the regional department of the ministry, whereas at the level of the local government, it mostly cooperated with the Executive Board. All of the witnesses, both of the Prosecution and of the Defence, testified to this effect and all of them claimed that this organ was competent for that, this organ headed by Bozo Ninkovic. During the trial, the Trial Chamber pointed out that special weight will be assigned to written evidence. We interpret this to mean that if they remain -- if they're consistent with the testimony of witnesses, then all of that will go to support the facts that under 1 could be forgotten, and under 2, represent something that could not have been directly found out by the witness, but this witness rather made his conclusions out of context. A typical example supporting this is the episode with woodcutting, which we analysed in detail in our brief, also referring to the relationship between the Executive Board, Ministry of Defence, and secretariat for economy and the work brigade. However, since the Prosecution failed to mention these documents, I will now use the following few minutes to point out to the Trial Chamber something that must be clear and something that the Prosecutor chose to forget. Document D92/1. The Prosecution referred to it in its final closing arguments. The decision of the Executive Board, dated 18th of September, 1992, on organising fall, autumn works. I would like to ask both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to read in detail Article 1, Article 3, as well as Article 9, and especially the order accompanying it. Document D112/3 -- no. I apologise. D112/1, which is a letter to the Executive Board by the department of Ministry of Defence. I will quote the document to my colleague Mr. Di Fazio. Document 137/1. Again, the same applies here. Document 137/1. The order of the Executive Board to the coordinator of the work defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The document previous to this one was 131/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see any written evidence which makes a link between the civilian defence staff and the forced labour. The Prosecution doesn't know what to do with its argument concerning forced labour, and they have to somehow incriminate my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can we just go back to your mentioning of the two documents? Because we are not sure what the interpreter means when she says the previous one was 131/1. Can you just refer to their numbers, the last two documents you discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters once again. So the document before the last one was D131/1, whereas the last document is D137/1, which is a letter of the Executive Board, dated 25th of September, 1992. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This task which the Prosecution assigned to itself required a lot of instances of combining various facts, a lot of instances of strange logic, and something to which we referred yesterday, which is taking out the words out of context, especially when it comes to the forced labour and the role which Tadic played in that respect. This is where they invested a lot of work. I would have to observe the following: This thesis linking the civilian defence staff with forced labour and looting is something that occurred to the Prosecutor at the end of the trial, when they realised that they had nothing in their hands. None of their witnesses, except for Nusret Hadzijusufovic, was asked about whether Miroslav Tadic or civilian defence staff issued any instructions to them or coordinated forced labour. These witnesses of the Prosecution spent hours and days here testifying about forced labour and looting. The Prosecutor didn't ask any questions of this nature of Bozo Ninkovic, nor of Ljubo Vukovic, about the lists of shops that, according to the Prosecutor, were looted. They didn't ask it of Miroslav Tadic either. And then they remembered Hadzijusufovic and decided that that was the solution. It was better to have at least one witness who would explain in detail how very deeply Miroslav Tadic was involved in forced labour and looting explain in detail how very deeply Miroslav Tadic was involved in forced labour and looting. What else does the Prosecution need? They need to take out of the context the facts related to some witnesses who are linked to Tadic. The Prosecutor mentions that people were frequently taken out of forced labour by the civilian defence staff, supporting this with the statement of Vukovic,who described the inventory of goods in shops. However, they are forgetting that, according to Vukovic, this task lasted for some ten days and that he was given several workers to complete this. The only witness of the Prosecution describing this episode is Nusret Hadzijusufovic, who spent one whole day working on this. You can take a look at page 6904 of the transcript regarding this. The Prosecutor then goes on to state that people were frequently engaged by the civilian defencestaff to change window panes on the houses that have been damaged during shelling, including the health centre, hospital, and so on. We don't know how often this was done and we don't know what the Prosecutor means when they state this. However, the Defence will say that they accept thesewords and that Miroslav Tadic is proud of these facts. If this constitutes a crime against humanity, then he is prepared to take the consequences on behalf of all of the people who were involved in repairing homes, houses, and organising shelters. Repairing homes to all citizens of Samac is something that has been frequently mentioned, especially with regard to mens rea concerning persecution. This is something that Witness Vukovic testified about. The Prosecution did not deny this; however, they, in their brief, stated that this should be taken as a mitigating factor, whereas yesterday in their closing arguments they said that there shouldn't be any mitigating factors for Tadic. However, in their brief, they said that it should be considered as a mitigating factor that he helped with organising shelters. A few days ago we heard from the Prosecution a new thesis that the civilian defence staff appropriated stolen goods or appropriated construction material, and they used the witness of Volasovic's statement to support this. I would like the Prosecution in their response to tell us where is it that Mr. Volasevic stated something of this nature, because we couldn't find that in the transcript. However, we could find the testimony of Vukovic, who stated that they applied to the Executive Board to be given glass for window panes, and there is also an exhibit, D113/3, which is aletter by the civilian defence staff sent to the Executive Board and asking for glass to be provided by the Uniglas company, which is a glass manufacturing company. The Prosecution [as interpreted] depicts Miroslav Tadic as this central figure of forced labour, and this false thesis is further attempted to be supported by the testimonies of Vukovic, Volasevic, and Hadzijusufovic. However, the Prosecution neglects numerous testimonies of testimonies ofother witness who deny this and which are in conformity with the testimonies of Vukovic and Volasevic. In their final brief the Prosecution gave a detailed analysis of the tesimony of Hadzijusufovic, both with respect to the work obligation and looting. I apologise. I said the Defence, but it says here the Prosecution, page 22, line 16. No. I apologise. Page 22, line 20, I said Defence there. I apologise. We don't have to go into detail with respect to the thesis of the Prosecution as to whether Hadzijusufovic was not truthful. However, we have reasons to believe that he lied fully aware of that. The problem with his testimony is that he is a completely incompetent witness. The fact thatthe Prosecution depicts him as a slave picturesquely and that he couldn't have known all of the regulations and documents, this is something that shows us what kind of witness the Prosecution is using to build their thesis upon. Let me remind the Trial Chamber. Hadzijusufovic is somebody who does not know that the secretariat for People's Defence exists and then all of a sudden he remembered that it did exist. Then he claimed that that secretariat did not exist during the wars then he didn't know who was Milos Bogdanovic, what Bozo Ninkovic was involved in, he didn't know what civilian defence was but he knew for a fact that Miroslav Tadic was the main person involved in forced labour and looting. Based on what? Based on hearsay evidence and testimony. That is quite impressive. The Prosecutor is fully aware of this and that's why they need reinforcement. And this is something that we shall turn to now. The thesis and taking out of context the testimonies of Vukovic and Volasevic, this is what they're using. Now, all of the evidence concerning the inventory and the list of things that the people from civilian defence were involved in and something that Vukovic testified to. Vukovic and Volasevic claimed that the list, complete list of shops, including some 15 to 16 shops in early May of 1992 existed and that vacant shops were inventoried, including three pharmacies of the companies from Serbia, which had perishable goods and dangerous chemicals and other items. This job lasted for 10 to 12 days and that following that, the civilian protection staff had nothing more to do with any sort of activities involving any kinds of goods. They said that this job had been organised by the Executive Board and that the establishment of that commission entailed peopleappointed by the Executive Council and not people from the Tadic's civilian defence staff, as the Prosecution claims. Since the Prosecutor did not challenge the testimony of Vukovic, nor did they ask him anything about the list of shops, then they attempted, in cross-examining Volasevic, on page 17765, to get an answer concerning these activities. However, Volasevic confirmed, just like Vukovic did, exactly what kind of goods these were, why they were put away, and this is something that the Prosecutor forgot to put in their final brief. The Prosecution, when referring to Vukovic and Volasevic, also forgot to mention that this was one single job or task that was completed in ten days. The Prosecution failed to mention that Hadzijusufovic was involved in this, for just one day, and that even he himself said that the inventory of goods was made on that occasion, and this was in full accord with testimonies of Defence witnesses who confirmed that this was one single task which was done competently and had nothing to do with looting. What is more indicative are other pieces of evidence and testimonies which the Prosecution is ignoring, fully disregarding the numerous pieces of evidence showing who was in charge of the forced labour. What the Prosecution is ignoring is that all of the rest of the witnesses of theProsecution came here and testified for many days about the forced labour, including labour. We will mention them. Within the work platoon, as direct participants, the following witnesses testified: Witness L, Witness M, Witness K, Esad Dagovic, Kemal Mehinovic, Witness E, Witness C, Witness Hajrija Drljacic, Ediba Bobic. All of these witnesses knew Miroslav Tadic from before the war. All of these witnesses had direct contacts with him. Some of them even saw him in front of the pensioners' centre. Some like M came to his headquarters and spent time there. I will admit that some of them did not favour my client, so therefore were not likely to forget anything regarding Tadic's activities. However, none of these witnesses ever mentioned that Miroslav Tadic and his civilian protection staff had any role in work obligation. The Prosecutors never asked any one of these witnesses concerning Miroslav Tadic and forced labour, and when they asked some of them who was responsible for that, who was in charge of that, they would invariably get the answer saying that the department of People's Defence was in charge ofthat and Bozo Ninkovic. All written evidence supports this, and what is most bizarre for the Prosecution is that this is also confirmed by Mr. Bozo Ninkovic. Aware of all of this, the Prosecutor has to engage in yet another construction and then allegedly the civilian protection was one of the major beneficiaries as far as the work brigade was concerned, and yet again this cannot be supported by any of the evidence proffered, because not a single witness except for Hadzijusufovic confirmed this. And what he saidwas that he worked only for one day. As opposed to this construction made by the OTP, their witnesses say what they did, who they worked for, and where they worked. When they do not have the evidence needed to support their statements, then they again start constructing things, and they say that the civilian defence staff and this part of the Ministry of Defence were in the same building, in order to facilitate cooperation, and then they say that both ofthese institutions were headed by members of the Crisis Staff. The Prosecutor forgets the evidence that points to the fact that there was a single telephone in that building. Now, how did Hadzijusufovic make any conclusions when Celic allegedly said to him that orders were coming from above? In the closing arguments, we heard yet another interesting thesis in this respect from the Prosecution, namely, that Tadic could, by way of his own authority, issue orders tocoordinators of work obligation, that he had something to do with sending workers to the separation and to build bunkers. The Prosecutor refuses to read the statements of Vukovic and Volasevic, that they were carrying telephone messages to Kapetanovic and Celic and that Tadic could not give any orders to anyone. Your Honours, please look at 14633. As for building bunkers, they quote the Defence allegedly, that they refer to Tubakovic and Ninkovic, whereas the Defence precisely referred in paragraph 273 to the fact that Radovan Antic was in charge of this particular work and that he was given this work force in the secretariat forNational Defence. Please look at pages 16767 and 16770. What is also forgotten is that all the evidence that was presented and that relates to the parties that used the work brigade, this civilian protection staff of Miroslav Tadic was certainly one of the beneficiaries that needed, so to speak, people the least. And it was not for their ownbenefit but for the benefit of the citizens of Samac. Then the Prosecutor goes on to describe work obligation and what various witnesses did, and he refers to the statements made by witnesses that we've just mentioned. But there is no reference whatsoever to Miroslav Tadic or his staff any longer. The same goes for the analysis of forcedlabour and plundering in relation to Odzak. There is no reference whatsoever to Tadic or his staff. Then they only refer to the cleaning of streets, the cleaning of houses, hard labour, in paragraph 245. And then in the footnote, they mention all these witnesses that I mentioned a short while ago, not to go through all of that again. Please look at all these statements, Your Honours. Please look at these footnotes and see whether there's any mention of Miroslav Tadic there whatsoever. Unless the Prosecution thinks that Witness K, who mentioned a lady called Mara, nicknamed Brka, the one with the moustache, is that who was meant, or was it Tadic who was meant? Bozo Ninkovic apparently is not such a bad witness for the Prosecution. It's not like they first treated him. They always refer to him when they want to say something about my client. The Prosecution refers to Ninkovic's statement in paragraph 248, that the representatives of the civilianprotection directly spoke to officials that had to deal with work obligation, Ninkovic was good for that, as far as they were concerned. However, Bozo Ninkovic does not say that the civilian defence had the authority to take workers without approval given by the secretariat for NationalDefence and Valosevic explained that these workers were under the Ministry of Defence and they had to address their request to them, and I'm referring to the civilian protection staff. However, taking these statements out of context and out of their entirety, the Prosecution omitts those parts of Ninkovic's statement that have to do with the following: That the Ministry of Defence was in charge of work obligation. Please look at the transcript 13680. And that Miroslav Tadic, or rather, his civilian defence staff, could not give any orders to anyone. Please look at page 13549 yet again. That is the kind of evaluation of evidence that is offered by the Prosecution, according to the following principle: I take what suits me. A witness lies a bit and then does not lie and then is a bit forgetful or, on the other hand, has a good memory. And all of this is supposed to serve their ultimate objective. And finally, in relation to the claims made by the Prosecution that has to do with shop lists. May I conclude by saying that the Prosecutor, through an incompetent, tendentious statement made by Hadzijusufovic, which I underline was contradictory to all other statements, tried to portray in a completely different way work that was conscientious,professional, and well done, such as making lists of shops in May, and they constructed this to mean that this had to do with forced labour and looting. An important aspect of the work of Miroslav Tadic through the civilian protection staff, which was not his protection staff, it was the civilian protection for all citizens of Samac; the Prosecutor is trying to discredit him yet again without wishing to accept clear evidence that they did not challenge and that is that this civilian protection staff wasengaged in doing one of the most useful jobs that could be done for the citizens of Samac. The Prosecution shoot themselves in the foot when they say that Miroslav Tadic was the key man related to forced labour, when in paragraph 253 they say that they -- that Simo Zaric was involved. And they are trying to involve Simo Zaric in forced labour as such, and this has to do with aSnjezana Delic episode. If Tadic were such a powerful man, why would he have to talk to Simo Zaric and ask him about this? If, according to the Prosecution, Miroslav Tadic was the main person in charge of forced labour, according to what logic espoused by the Prosecution would he have toconvey to Simo Zaric this request made by Snjezana Delic? The Prosecution invokes of testimony of Snjezana Delic and interprets things that they did not even ask her about. In their construction, why did the Prosecution not quote the statement of Delic and when she testified that MiroslavTadic said that he was not the one who decided about that? The Defence believes that the answer to this question is quite clear, quite simply, this did not suit the Prosecution. On the basis of everything I've said so far and which was particularly emphasised in our final brief, the Defence claims that the Prosecution did not offer a shred of evidence that can prove beyond a reasonable doubt to the Trial Chamber that Miroslav Tadic was criminally liable in any way,according to Article 7(1). Your Honours, I wanted to speak about looting, but in view of the time frame, I'm just going to say a few words. If the Court finds that Miroslav Tadic has nothing to do with forced labour and looting under quotation marks, if I can put it that way, then he is not certainly culpable as far as this particular count is concerned either. I would like to drawthe attention of the Trial Chamber to another thing, document P88, whereby the Prosecution wants to link up the crisis -- the civilian defence staff with the lists of shops, and this is supposed to be crown evidence in terms of plundering. There is no reference to what the civilian protectionstaff actually did. There is not a shred of evidence that the civilian protection staff took part in the organisation of establishing warehouses, and this is what the Prosecution claims. Their key witness, Hadzijusufovic, their key witness for forced labour, says that these goods were stored in Agrooprema, and this document, P88, talks about two completely different warehouses, may I remind you of that, one in Obudovac, one in Samac. And these are goods that have to be taken out of a zone of war operations and this has nothing to do whatsoever with what they are trying to say and they are trying to link the civilian protection staff to that. Your Honours, I'm now going to move on to a subject that we worked on the most in our final brief. After all, I see that the Prosecutor has devoted quite a few pages of their final brief to that subject and that is deportation, forcible expulsions, and relocations. It is obvious that this count in the indictment, in terms of how the Prosecution sees the role of the commission for exchanges and the role of Miroslav Tadic in this commission, is a particularly important part of the indictment. This was the reason why during the proceedings we called a significant number of witnesses to testify about exchanges. Why we offered to the Trial Chamber such a large number of documents and other evidence. Finally, this is why we decided to focus on that in our final brief as well. As for the definition of deportation, forcible relocation, and expulsion, we gave our legal analysis in terms of the similarities and dissimilarities in our final brief. So I'm not going to refer to that at all. However, I am going to say a few words about something that I heard from the Prosecutor in their closing arguments, and I think that this is contentious from the point of view of the Defence. Namely, I'm referring to the thesis that all persons who were expelled from the country were expelled primarily to Croatia, another state. The exchanges, if they are indeed deportation acts, as the Prosecution claims, have a special characteristic. These exchanges were carried out and negotiated with commissions of the HVO, for the most part, also with Muslim commissions and, up to a certain extent, with commissions of the Republic of Croatia. This primarily refers to the detained Serbs, and you have documents to that effect. Almost all Prosecution witnesses confirmed that from the places where the exchanges took place, primarily Dragalic and Lipovac, and we heard about that, they went to Orasje for the most part. At first they mentioned Odzak. Both of these towns were under HVO control. Therefore, the final destination of these persons - I repeat, final destination - was within Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it was under the control of different authorities, another authority. Reference to this is made in the Krstic and Naletilic cases. As for these facts, there is evidence proffered by Osman Jasarevic, Jelena Kapetanovic, Esad Dagovic, Witness A. In this connection, we challenge the claims made by the Prosecution in paragraph 101, because all persons who were exchanged went via Croatia, and all negotiations in relation to the victims from Samac were with the HVO and we know that this is the Croatian community of the Croatian Posavina. Persons who went to the state of Croatia or via the state of Croatia to third countries, in view of the form that was required by the state of Croatia - please recall the letters of guarantee - had the status of persons, citizens, who were going to visit someone, because it was only on that condition that they could stay on Croatian territory, and we wrote about this in detail in our final brief. In our final brief, at the very outset, we presented the views of Miroslav Tadic in relation to exchanges, and also his position as far as exchanges were concerned, and I should like to focus on that now. Miroslav Tadic was involved in exchanges after a large number of Serbs were detained in the municipality of Odzak in May 1992. Several thousand are mentioned in this context. Throughout this period, after that, he worked on exchanges. Starting from October 1992, he became a member of the municipal commission for exchanges. The exchanges that he took part in were not unlawful or involuntary. They were carried out on the basis of principles that were applied and established by the International Red Cross. Exchanges as carried out by the Samac commission were not a vehicle for persecution but a vehicle for exercising free choice of individuals in terms of whether they would stay or leave from a particular territory, whether they would like to go to the territory that was under the control of the other side. People who worked on the basis of such principles in these exchanges were engaged in humane endeavours, with the objective of helping all, irrespective of ethnic background. Miroslav Tadic and the commission did not have the authority to ask personally and to decide whether somebody could be exchanged or not. Miroslav Tadic could not stop anyone through his own free will or coerce anyone to go for an exchange. The commission for exchanges was not receiving any instructions or was it involved in any plan or cooperation for carrying out this final state of ethnic cleansing of the territory. Written evidence was provided, as well as verbal testimony, that through this commission, over 800 detainees and civilians left the municipality of Samac and also that about 140 to 150 went through military commissions. They were detainees who left Batkovic. But this was not under the Samac commission. As regards this count in the indictment, again we have to deal with figures, because the indictment is based on figures. In paragraph 295, the Prosecution refers to statistical indicators, and also the report of Mr. Robert Donia, then their demography experts. This is P133. And the report of the Special Rapporteur of the United Nations, dated the 17th of November, 1993. However, what the Prosecutor forgot in his final brief is that by way of evidence there is also the expert opinion of Professor Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic. The Defence knows why. Therefore, I shall have to refer in a few words to statistical expertise, although I wrote about it in detail in our final brief. The task of both experts, the expert of the Defence and of the Prosecution, was to assist all of us, notably the Trial Chamber, to establish whether, in the period of the indictment, there were ethnic changes in the pattern of the population in the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Odzak. What did the Prosecution offer the Trial Chamber through the expert opinions of their own experts? Ewa Tabeau, for instance, an expert for death rates, for mortality, for death rates, does not know that in the census of 1991, the workers working abroad temporarily were also included. It was only later that she stated that this was possible. She carries out an analysis by comparing citizens and taking into account the different areas covered by the municipality, the area covered before the war and after the war. She includes whole villages, Muslim-populated villages in although they were not in the municipality in 1991 - they were not living there at that time - in order to increase the number of non-Serbs in the municipality. And yet, during cross-examination, when this let me say manipulation was found out, she admits that she made a mistake and after being ordered by the Trial Chamber, she inserts corrections into her work, and excludes from her analysis about a third of the population of the municipality of Samac and almost half of the Odzak population, adding that they lived in divided settlements. Then she goes on and draws the final conclusion, that ethnic cleansing was carried out of the municipalities of Samac and Odzak Vukosavlje, ethnic cleansing, an extensive one, and she goes as far as to say that this was the most extensive example of ethnic cleansing, the most extensive instance of ethnic cleansing in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It took only several questions by laymen, the Defence counsel, to show that her tables, Exhibit P133, shows the percentage of ethnic cleansing of Serbs from Odzak as much higher, because as she shows, there were only 0.48 per cent Serbs left there, as opposed to the 3.000 voters that were there in 1991. In 1997, there were only 28 of those left. However, according to the objective analysis by this expert, this does not deserve to be labelled as ethnic cleansing, let alone extensive ethnic cleansing. Her analysis was entitled "changes to the ethnic make-up of the population," not changes to the ethnic make-up of the Croats and Muslims. So much for her. Svetlana Radovanovic, an expert for demographic analysis, a Defence witness, drew a different conclusion. She concluded that there were no reliable statistical data that could show with accuracy how the ethnic make-up of the population was made, if we look at the same territory before and after the Dayton Accords without singling out settlements or rather at municipal level. The ethnic make-up of the population in these areas is the same in 1997 as it was before the war, according to her. She is a professor of demographic analysis, but she did not think herself competent enough to announce ethnic cleansing. She provided a very accurate and detailed analysis of the sources of population censuses and the reports by OSCE, which she considers not as reliable sources but rather as very flimsy sources. Both of these experts, however, agreed on one thing: That if we employ statistical methods, there is no way for us to ascertain how and to what extent the structure, the ethnic make-up of the population changed in the period between 1991 and 1993, which is an essential thing and which is key to this criminal procedure, because we are, after all, acting before a criminal court. If we leave these experts statisticians aside and leave their findings in the drawers, although I do have several interesting theses and observations connected with how people declared themselves in terms of ethnic backgrounds. Once we do that, what do we have to do? We have to rely on other testimonies, on the testimonies of other witnesses, an issue we have also addressed in our final brief. Having no other evidence of the change in the ethnic make-up in Samac, the Prosecution has found a different solution by referring to sections of the report of the Special Rapporteur which actually relate to other parts of Republika Srpska and does not even mention the municipalities of Samac and Odzak. We read in the Prosecution's trial brief about some villages that no one in this case has ever heard of. This is supposed to be a new method of criminal procedure called analogy. One uses the report by the Special Rapporteur which is not a well-known fact under Rule 94, dated 17th November, 1993. I would have liked the Prosecution to clarify something about their final brief, because I believe that this document, unlike the other two, was not tendered into evidence during the trial, although it was tendered under Rule 94, as a well-known fact. The Defence still believes that even if it is a well-known fact, this document can only be tendered and admitted into evidence during the trial itself, so as to be formally acknowledged by the Trial Chamber. That's what the Rules say. If the Prosecution failed to tender it into evidence during the trial itself, during the evidentiary proceedings, I ask of the Trial Chamber to disregard that document. What did the Defence offer in terms of figures? A method often employed by the Prosecution, talking about figures. When media covered this trial, there was talk of extensive ethnic cleansing, which was a quote from the indictment. Now we had this spectacular figure of 22.000 inhabitants of the Odzak municipality, and what's left of that now? You've heard the evidence. They all left in an organised manner before the Army of Republika Srpska even arrived in the territory. Eight thousand inhabitants of Bosanski Samac never budged from where they were. Those were mostly Croats and Muslims. Because they ended up in the other entity, of the divided municipality. And both experts, the Prosecution and our own expert agreed on this. 4.500 inhabitants of the Croat villages left prior to the 17th and 18th of April and during those two days, in 1992. We've had a number of witnesses testifying to this. I will not now go on to mention their names, but they are in our trial brief. Stjepan Blazanovic evacuated about 250 men in early May. So much for the figures. So much for the expert opinions. The Prosecutor refers to a large number of testimonies of witnesses who they asked whether, on the 17th of April, they wanted to leave Samac, forgetting that many of those witnesses clearly said that they had put their families away somewhere safe prior to the 17th of April. The Prosecutor refuses to see that what we're talking about is a rational fear, fear of war, fear of war operations. The Defence has addressed this issue in detail in our final brief. We also emphasise that a significant number of Serb families also left prior and during the war, as mentioned by my colleague Pantelic yesterday. The Prosecutor then refers to a number of witnesses who said they had no intention of leaving Bosanski Samac but were forced to do so. I think this may be a convenient time for a break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a correction to make with regard to the transcript. My colleague Pantelic suggested that instead of the term ethnic make-up, we should be using the term "ethnic composition." And on page 37, line 24 when I referred to Stjepan Blazanovic, I said "and his sabotage group from Croatia." This was something not reflected in the transcript. I will pick up where I left off talking about the allegations of the Prosecution. The Prosecutor referred to several witnesses, saying that they had no intention of leaving Samac but rather that they were forced to leave Samac. The Prosecutor, however, refuses to quote witnesses who were free to leave Bosanski Samac but didn't, who prior to the 17th of April, 1992, lived in Samac and still live there. Although the Prosecutor wishes to minimise their number, during this trial, we heard live testimony from a number of those witnesses, which I will now not name individually. In paragraph 300, the Prosecutor refers to testimonies regarding the several ways to leave Samac. The Defence team has addressed this in our final brief, and we invoke those facts with regard to the same testimonies that were invoked by the Prosecution. However, the only thing that the Prosecution considers important is to use this to prove their allegation that those different ways to leave Samac only applied to non-Serbs. The Prosecutor forgets the testimonies telling us that the Serbs too were using their privately owned vehicles to put their families away and take them to a safe place, that there was a huge convoy, a bus convoy, of probably the same buses that were later used for the exchanges. On those buses, there were many mixed families who left for Serbia in mid-May. The Prosecution forgets that the Serbs too had to falsify documents and authorisations to leave Samac. They should look at Zeljko Volasevic's testimony to reassure themselves. When the Prosecutor speaks about different ways to leave the territory individually, they refer to the testimony of Witness E, who was forbidden to leave town in the first days of war, but his wife and children did leave. The Prosecution, however, refuses to refer to the continuation of the same testimony by Witness E, the very next sentence. In fact, where Witness E says that his Serb neighbour who was with him in the car was also not allowed to pass through the checkpoint, and the nationality of his neighbour was clearly pointed out. Please have a look at page 7665 of the transcript. And now for the exchanges. The Defence asserted that the legal way, and I'm saying this without inverted commas, without quotation marks, the legal way for persons who wanted to leave the Samac territory and cross to the territory held by a different entity or state, the legal way was a procedure called exchange. The Defence in their final brief clarified why these exchanges were not at all for the violation of fundamental human rights, but rather a tool for exercising those same rights; not persecution, but rather humanitarian work. The Prosecution seems to have a problem with that because they avoid addressing some key issues raised by the Defence or rather address them very briefly only. What they are left with are auxiliary methods. The first way they wish to challenge the procedure of these exchanges was bribery and money that was offered in order to be exchanged. The first thing I would like to point out is that we analysed in detail in our final brief, testimonies with regard to the charges of bribery. As far as this issue is concerned, we are in the middle of a criminal procedure and there is a need to compare testimonies for the Trial Chamber, for the Court to be able to reach an unequivocal conclusion. The Prosecution has already referred to witnesses analysed by the Defence, but what we can say in a general way is that those witnesses were mutually contradictory and exclusive, and mutually exclusive. The only thing we can glean from those testimonies is rumour, hearsay, always including a different detail discrediting their whole story, their whole testimony. All the witnesses who referred to that particular incident - I'm talking about the incident involving Sabah Seric - left through an exchange, were exchanged and left Batkovici, without paying any fee to anyone. Some of those witnesses left during the very first exchanges, from Batkovici such as Witness C and Witness E, a month or two after they arrived in Batkovici. All those who refer to the incident described it in different ways, and in this multitude of details, discrepancies became obvious during cross-examination. Can we please go into private session for a moment, for the benefit of protected witnesses and their identities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction. This refers to witnesses who are not protected witnesses, Hajrija Drljacic and Hasan Subasic. It appears, however, that these witnesses did not discuss details. They all seemed to remember these details in a whole lot of different ways, as to when exactly this happened, whose names were called out, and how the whole thing developed. There is something unequivocal and something that is not convenient for the Prosecution. There are exchange lists showing that Sabah Seric was on one of those lists and there was a clear procedure to leave Batkovici and to get approval to leave, of which there is ample evidence on the part of the Defence and which the Prosecution turns a blind eye to. There is also the testimony of Makso Simeunovic, one of the favourite Defence witnesses in the eyes of the Prosecution. There is the testimony of Grujicic, and now the question I'm asking is: Did Tadic really have so much authority as to be able to influence the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the military prosecutor, or any of the security bodies by merely taking from Seric one or two hundred German marks and this is where a discrepancy occurs between the testimonies. How come that Hasan Subasic followed the testimony via the Internet and claims that the event took place as both Witness M and Kemal Mehinovic claimed in the course of 1993? These were testimonies in open session. We all know beyond a shadow of a doubt, and I mean Sabah Seric, that he left on the 24th of December, 1992. This has not been challenged. We know because a witness said this in closed session, so Mr. Subasic, when he was following the testimony on the Internet, was not in a position to hear this. Yesterday, we heard a new evidence. We don't know which witness said it, in fact, so I would like to ask the Prosecutor to tell us who said it, that Tadic received gold, jewellery, and other valuables. We never heard a word mentioned about this during the trial. The Prosecutor referred to Hajrija Drljacic, which is their main hearsay witness, concerning everything that took place in the Samac municipality. Her testimony concerning bribery is devoid of any significance except when it comes to rumours, and I do not deny that. Her entire testimony involving a large number of facts was based on secondhand information or hearsay. She claimed herself that during her stay in Samac she heard nothing of bribery but that she heard that later, after she was exchanged. However, she claimed that bribery was an open secret. What is something that cannot be denied is that none of the witnesses who were in Batkovici ever claimed that they gave money to Tadic then, and all of them later came to be exchanged. The Defence did not deny rumours concerning offering of the bribery. The Prosecution has no evidence to support this, and in their final closing arguments, they are supporting this by rumours. The Defence decided to mention the words of His Honour Judge Singh who was a member of this Trial Chamber and who said during the trial: Are we go to have evidence of rumours? This is a criminal court. Another witness in this courtroom, when pressed by the Prosecutor to confirm bribery, said: I cannot confirm that this man took money. Rumours are rumours, and facts are facts. This was stated by Kemal Bobic, the man who did not want to support even the testimony of his own wife, precisely because of these rumours, and he gave an oath, a solemn declaration, just like all other witnesses. This entire story with rumours does have a logic of its own, and the Defence sees it in quite a different story of Miroslav Tadic mentioned during his testimony. When explaining his work in exchanges, he in one emotional moment, I will call it, said as follows, and I will paraphrase this: Everybody considered me to be guilty, or everybody blamed me, those who had arrived, those whom I couldn't bring here, those who died and didn't manage to come here, as well as those who were exchanged and got killed afterwards. All of them blamed me. Perhaps somebody would not make a link between these two stories. However, the Defence is convinced that due to a dislike that some people felt with respect to Miroslav Tadic, as well as with respect to all other people who were involved in this great, important task, that this is what caused these rumours about bribery. I don't think that the Prosecution managed to prove anything beyond reasonable doubt as to any link between Miroslav Tadic and the bribery. Now, as to whether residents were asked whether they wanted to be exchanged, that's a different topic. The Prosecution said that some of the witnesses never were asked whether they wanted to be exchanged or not, but they were simply told to get ready. Witness A and Witness C, and Delic Dragan. However, the Defence witnesses given by people who were involved in exchange, as well as some witnesses of the Prosecution, stated that all of the people had to state whether they wanted to cross over or not at the exchange line. They were asked by the Red Cross representatives whether they wanted to be exchanged, and this is something that Dragan Lukac testified to, as did Witness M and Vasovic. However, the Prosecution forgot to mention that witnesses who had been sought by somebody else were asked whether they wanted to cross or not. The Prosecutor referred to testimony of Dragan Delic, who said that nobody asked him whether he wanted to be exchanged. However, they neglected the testimony of his wife Snjezana, who said that she went to the Red Cross several times and talked to Tadic, asking that her husband be exchanged. What is essentially important is what has been proven, which is that a large number of these people had been sought by the other side, somebody on the other side wanted them to come to the exchange line, where they had to expressly state whether they wanted to cross or stay at home. So the only thing needed was the permission from police and military security organs during the time they were detained in Samac, and only upon the permission being issued by these authorities and if these individuals had been sought by other side, regardless of whether they had been sought by families or not. Sometimes they were sought by authorities on the other side. Therefore, only upon all of these conditions these people had to state whether they wanted to be exchanged or not at the exchange line. The Prosecution claims that Tadic was the architect of the exchanges. We have to state once again that he was involved together with other people between May and October 1992. Perhaps he was the most high profile among them. However, he was not the one who made decisions, which is the way the Prosecution depicts him. Tadic does not want to denigrate his work in exchanges. He simply wants to put it in a factual framework. The Prosecution wants to use typical constructions in order to deny this. On page 46, line 1, I said that Tadic was the person -- perhaps -- the person who figured perhaps the most prominently in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we suggest that the use of term "exposed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For which one? Because he said he was the most --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For Mr. -- For what -- for the term that Mr. Lukic used here, instead of word "perhaps he was the most high profile among them," on page 45, line 25, and page 46, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleague Lazarevic. When in their brief in footnote 831 the Prosecution refers to that statement, they do not want the Trial Chamber to take into account the continuation of that part of testimony of Mr. Tadic which pertains to the fact that in October 1992 the formal decision on the commission for exchange was made, why was a man who until that time was an informal president of an unexisting commission, then why did he not then become its president? And this is something that Todorovic and Jez were against, and many witnesses confirmed that, especially the testimony of Witness DW1/3. The written statement of that witness confirms that Tadic was replaced because he pleased Croats too frequently. The decision doesn't know why -- the Defence doesn't know why the Prosecution claimed that Miroslav Tadic was generally responsible for negotiations concerning the exchange of the citizens of Bosanski Samac and the mechanism of that. All of the evidence in this trial points clearly to the period of time and the level of his responsibility and competence when it comes to negotiations. This can be clearly gleaned from the notebook of the centre for information, which is a very clear evidence of the content of the negotiations. It clearly stems from that, that then, in 1992, Tadic could not make any decision because he did not have a consent from relevant authorities. Upon his appointment as member of the commission, the communication between the Samac commission and other commissions, especially that of the 1st Krajina Corps and East Bosnia Corps, which were military commissions and pertained to prisoners which fell under the jurisdiction of those military commissions, therefore, any communication between them went through the president of the commission, which can be gleaned from correspondence between Grujicic and Maslic, some four or five documents that have been admitted into evidence and fully explained. Wishing to raise their thesis on joint criminal enterprise to a higher level, and especially that about persecution as well, the Prosecution tries to show that there was a link there with respect to exchanges and involvement of institutions. It is clear to the Defence that there was a certain framework of that cooperation and evidence was introduced to support this. We have already mentioned the procedure in Batkovici. And in addition to that, we also claim that as long as people were held in detention in Samac, certain institutions and exchanges were linked only as a result of the fact that a conditional consent was needed. It was not cooperation, as the Prosecution claims. It was not a cooperation, because Tadic could not take anybody out of detention and have that person exchanged without receiving prior to that a consent from police, security organs, and later on from the military, General Staff, military judiciary, and military prosecutor. The only term to describe this would be that this was done upon conditional consent. Todorovic testified about this; however, the Prosecutor chose not to quote that. When asked explicitly by the Defence counsel of Tadic, Todorovic stated that not a single person was taken out by Miroslav Tadic without prior police consent. The Defence doesn't understand why is it, if not wanting to make a link between various institutions and exchanges, why does then the Prosecution mention centre for social work and then calls that centre Tadic's centre?
