Are they trying to increase the significance of the role of Tadic? Are they speculating that Tadic had something to do with the centre when in fact he did not? Nor did the centre have anything to do with these exchanges. The facts speak to the contrary, and they are quite accurate when describing how is it that this was place where people signed up for exchanges. Witness Maslic stated that the Red Cross received messages through the International Red Cross and then sent it on to the families. This was confirmed by Milka Petrovic, and there is also written correspondence to prove this between -- written correspondence between local Red Cross chapters within Republika Srpska and elsewhere. It is logical that this is where people came to sign up in order to leave, but this is also a place where people came to report that they wanted to leave during the evacuation in May of 1992, as well as in following evacuations, which unfortunately did not take place. This is something that Volasevic, Tadic, and Vukovic testified about. It is clear that the job of the local Red Cross was not only to have a list of people who wanted to be exchanged but that this is where people came to get information concerning their departure. Sveto Vasovic confirmed this in his testimony. The Prosecution stated that Miroslav Tadic was the one who decided who was to be exchanged, and once again, they are taking out of context the testimony of Mrs. Snjezana Delic. In footnote 841, she, Snjezana Delic, said that she went to sign up with the Red Cross in order to find Tadic, who was in charge, and in order to convey her request to him. However, in that part of the transcript, he -- she had previously stated that she knew that the Red Cross was where people went to sign up for exchanges and that she went to talk to Tadic, who told her that it wasn't a problem for her and the children to leave, but, however, there was a problem for her husband to leave. And on that page, she stated exactly what Tadic had stated as to who decided on -- as to who decided on whether her husband was going to be exchanged or not. She does mention some Crisis Staff in Pelagicevo, and she is probably there referring to the security organ of the brigade which was stationed, the 2nd Posavina Brigade, which was stationed in Pelagicevo, and she also mentioned her personal knowledge about Todorovic being in charge of that. However, this is not a good ground for the Prosecution to conclude based on that that Tadic was the one who decided on departure of civilians. She referred to Hadzijusufovic and his conversation with Vasovic. However, on page 14972, Vasovic described in detail the process of citizens signing up themselves and giving their particulars and stating that they wished to leave. The procedure was such that these people then sent their request to the Red Cross and then the lists were sent on to Mr. Mihajlovic, who was president of the local Red Cross chapter, and that following that, the lists were taken elsewhere in order to get consent for that. What is essential concerning departure of individuals, I will say civilians who reported to the local Red Cross, was stated by people who were directly involved in those tasks, Maslic, Grujicic, Vasovic, and Simeunovic, and I have to say, Witness DW1/3 is especially important there, due to his credibility. The Prosecution doesn't mention this witness frequently because it doesn't suit them, but this witness stated that civilians went to the Red Cross to discuss their exchange, and if military commissions were involved in the exchange, then civilian commissions would frequently tell them that there was a need for civilians also to cross over and that this was usually done on the day of the exchange itself. Please take a look at page 14806 of the transcript. The Defence agrees to a large extent with the evidence referred to by the Prosecution which concerns the significant role of the police in the exchanges. Why was police security detail needed is fully explained by the episode of Witness A. This episode is also very relevant due to the fact that it describes the relationship between Tadic and Todorovic and his people. I've mentioned this episode yesterday as well. As for the significance and the role of the police in terms of exchanges, the Defence refer to this in their final brief. The Prosecution does refer to Todorovic, though, and he said that he was only asked about the release of smaller groups and that actually it was the Crisis Staff that decided about larger groups of prisoners and also important detainees. He, Todorovic, like in most of his testimony, tried to diminish his own importance in this way. Mr. Pantelic referred to this, and I draw your attention to that. However, as opposed to Todorovic, Svetozar Vasovic has no reason to lie or to heighten or lessen Todorovic's importance. He said quite clearly who was God almighty in Samac and that he, Vasovic, communicated exclusively with this God almighty as far as exchanges were concerned. This statement of Vasovic's coincides with the statements of all persons who could have had some knowledge about how approval was given for exchanges. Witness Vasovic and D156/3 both corroborate that. The only evidence on the basis of which the Prosecution wishes to draw Tadic into higher regional and state structures who are in charge of exchanges are the request to leave and for the members of the commission to move about, which was signed by Slobodan Markovic. Tadic is not even on that list, but Grujicic said later that he got this permit, too. However, this document only corroborates the thesis of the Defence that military negotiators and representatives of the civilian commissions went together to negotiations because these negotiations were are dangerous physically, as they entailed movement through territory where there were war operations going on. How does the Prosecution come to the conclusion that Maslic was the formal president of the commission and that Tadic was the most important member of the commission, even after October 1992? The Prosecution refers to the period before the 2nd of October and the testimony of DW1/3 is something that we quoted only a few minutes, and the Prosecution did not actually quote this witness. In its final brief, the Defence spoke about the activities of Tadic that were quite contrary to this trade that the Prosecution referred to. The Prosecution referred to cannon fodder, livestock trade, something to that effect. However, the exchange of Witnesses A and Q is telling evidence of this. Please look at all the lists of exchanges and you will see how many persons, Witness A was exchanged for and how many persons Witness Q was exchanged for. In footnote 913, the Prosecution refers to the status of detainees on the basis of the Mazowiecki report. However, the status of prisoners is precisely stipulated in documents of the International Red Cross. In 193/3,the International Red Cross states that a prisoner is, in relation to exchanges, a very specific category of people, and this same is referred to by the creators of the Dayton Agreement, Article 9, annex 1(a), paragraph 1. Also, the document of the ICRC dated the 24th of March, 1993, Prosecution Exhibit 179, refers to the same thing. This is an agreement concluded between the warring parties on the 1st of October, 1992, and this was done under the auspices of the ICRC. The same standards were applied when referring to detainees in terms of their release. But the term "mutual release" or "exchange" is used as well. The thesis of the Prosecution that in some documents the word "release" is referred to and that this is only the release of prisoners rather than exchange is also contrary to the written evidence, even that supplied by the Prosecution, because exchanges are referred to in that context as well. Also the term "mutual release" is nothing but exchange. The Defence believes that this kind of definition of the term "prisoner" was more broadly interpreted than in the Geneva Conventions and this was motivated precisely by humane reasons, so that status would not have these persons detained longer than necessary, and the proceedings involved were supposed to be brought to an end as quickly and as simply as possible. So it was again this humane endeavour that the commission was engaged in. The Defence, on the basis of all evidence presented, sees the acts of the Samac commission to be fully in line with these documents. The claim made about the cooperation between the military and civilian commissions is quite unfounded. The Prosecution says that they just geographically cover different regions. Again, this is a construction. What is essential is that as regards the prisoners from Batkovic, consent was given by the highest military, judicial, and security organs, and they gave this consent to military commissions only. This is referred to in documents D167/3, D170/3, D172/3, D173/3, D174/3. Also, this was testified to by the key persons involved in this, Maslic, Grujicic, Simeunovic, Witness DW1/3 as well. As for the document on the appointment of Mr. Grujicic as president of the commission, this was signed by General Talic, the Defence claims, and this is based on the testimony that the military commissions significantly assisted civilian commissions, and this is referred to in document D180/3as well. But please take a careful look at document D181/3, the letter that Grujicic sent to the International Red Cross. This also says that what is requested is to establish a corridor for the free flow of the civilian population. This document was written in June 1993. There were so many problems involved, due to war operations, and everybody wanted to have this established. Prosecution claims that Tadic often went to Batkovic. Tadic never denied that he had been to Batkovic a few times. Now, whether this happened often or a few times, it is for you to judge, Your Honours. Count how many times this happened between December 1992 and June 1993, and also he did not take part in some of this at all, and this was testified to by witnesses. The Defence stated clear-cut reasons that fully contest what was said about receiving bribes. However, what is shocking in the final brief is linking up the testimony of Grujicic that had to do with fuel and why Tadic paid for this fuel. My judicial opinion is that such constructions do not belong in criminal proceedings, and therefore, I am not going to make an effort to enter a polemic with this. Perhaps we can see how Tadic did make every effort for Witness A to be exchanged, and he opposed those hoodlums of Todorovic's. And the Prosecution constructed that Tadic had an interest to have the exchange carried out because there was money involved on his part. When challenging the positions of the Defence that have to do with exchanges, the Prosecution minimalises the Defence thesis. The Prosecution claims that only some persons were asked as to whether they wanted to be exchanged or not. The evidence states otherwise. Everybody stated their views as to whether they wanted to be exchanged or not. This was testified to by those who organised exchanges and those who were actually exchanged. Even Witness Hadzijusufovic, such a highly contentious witness, had to say that he had to state whether he wanted to be exchanged or not in the presence of UNPROFOR representatives. Also the testimony of Witness DW8/3 says that he did not say whether he wanted to be exchanged or not at the actual line, but that Tadic said that he should remain on the bus. Had they analysed - "they," the Prosecution - everything that took place on the 29th of January, 1993, in Lipovac, they would have seen why this was done, because all the witnesses said that this was a rather special exchange because the representatives were not allowed to be present in the UNPROFOR tent when the persons involved were actually stating their views. Tadic, simply fearful of what would happen, he said to the man who wanted to be exchanged: Just stay behind. And then he worked this out with the negotiators of the opposing side, without any problem whatsoever. So that is what the Prosecution does when they take things out of context. The Defence is perplexed by what the Prosecutor said in his final arguments. We have the impression that they are challenging what the Defence proved, that people were stating whether they wanted to be exchanged or not at the actual line of exchange and that on the other side they would say that they did not want to cross over. The Defence understands that these facts are disastrous for the Prosecution themselves, that they undermine their entire thesis about the exchanges as a vehicle for persecution, but we do not understand the arguments presented by the Prosecution, because both in the final brief and in the arguments, the Prosecution said that citizens after all did state their views at the exchange itself. Now, this is supposed to prove that Mladen Borbeli did not categorically state to the opposite side that they -- that he did not want to cross over, because he had to put it so categorically in order for the Prosecution to attach appropriate weight to it. But then why didn't the Prosecutor ask Witness Borbeli here in the courtroom, "why did you state this categorically?" Witness DW2/3 testified about how persistently the other side was seeking him and how much he had beseeched Tadic not to have him appear at the exchange line knowing that if he were to oppose crossing over to the other side he could create problems for himself being a reserve officer, and at that time his family. His family was already on the other side. This testimony is something that does not affect the Prosecutor. It doesn't mean a thing to the Prosecutor. Why doesn't the Prosecutor look at paragraph 11 of the 92 bis statement of Avdo Arslanovic? This is D123/3, who described how he was taken to the separation line in order to convince his own relative that he did not want to leave Samac. And do you know what happened to this Arslanovic, Mr. Prosecutor? Read his statement. You accepted this statement. You did not want to cross-examine him. You did not want to call him. You did not challenge anything at that point. This Arslanovic, had he come to testify here, to you, he would have told you that he lives in Samac, that he stayed in Samac, that he lives in Samac until the present day, and he would have told you about all the things that Tadic did for him and his family, this inhumane Miroslav Tadic. I don't have to specifically state the person concerned is a Muslim. Your Honours, please take a look at document D102/3, and the Prosecution may do so as well. These are minutes on the talks that were held in Gradacac between the Muslim and the Serb commission, and the members of the families who were stating their views there as to whether they wanted to be reunited with their families or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may remind you, your time is up, unless you would like to use your one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall really make an effort to speed up now. I will have to take time off that additional hour, then, and I'm going to see what the Prosecution is going to say to me and then I will see what I'll say in rebuttal and Mr. Pantelic tells me perhaps he'll give me a minute or two. The Prosecution invoked the Krnojelac judgement with regard to force, and this is not contested. This is part of the Statute of the International Criminal Court. However, from this same Krnojelac judgement, the Prosecution did not want to read a very interesting position put by the Trial Chamber and is only a few paragraphs after the one they quoted. What is said there: "There is general evidence that detainees wanted to be exchanged and that those selected for so-called exchanges freely exercised their choice to go and that they did not have to be forced. The Trial Chamber is not satisfied that the displacement of these individuals from Foca necessarily involved in the choice," their choice is something I underline, "was involuntary." This is paragraph 483 of the Krnojelac judgement. It has to do with the camp in Foca. Now, who was this who did not want to be exchanged from Samac? Your Honours, the Prosecution suggested to you that you put yourselves in the position of Snjezana Delic. This should certainly be done, but not in a one-sided manner. That, after all, is the mandate of this Trial Chamber, to evaluate all the evidence presented and to pass judgement. The Trial Chamber cannot only pass judgement by accepting what a witness said. The Court is going to evaluate this in the context of other evidence and other feelings. Your Honours, in the same way, you should put yourselves in the position of Dario Radic, who was arrested, who was detained, whose father was detained. Put yourself in the position of DW8/3, who was present when Todorovic killed Antesa in the SUP. What they went through and why they stayed behind. Finally, put yourselves in the position of Miroslav Tadic. Just a moment, please. I said Witness DW8/3, who was present in the SUP building when Todorovic killed Antesa. Finally, put yourselves in the skin of Miroslav Tadic. His colleague, Snjezana Delic, asked her -- asked him to help her concerning the exchange for her two children and her husband, who had been Tadic's student and Tadic could not help her. This is one of the images from this trial, this case, that you have to look at and evaluate when judging the merits of the case. It is only in that way that you can comprehensively look at the entirety of all of this. I'm just going to say a few more words about the International Red Cross and Miroslav Tadic and their relations. The Prosecution overrates the far-sightedness of Tadic's Defence as concerns the decision by the Court related to the International Committee of the Red Cross. Miroslav Tadic had a great interest in clarifying the role of the International Red Cross as concerns facts relevant for his Defence. Tadic testified on a number of occasions about his relationship with the International Red Cross. These interviews were released in 1998 and the Trial Chamber passed its decision as concerns the International Red Cross in 1999. Do you really believe we are so far-sighted as to know that the Trial Chamber would have a ruling on the International Red Cross and then continue to make constructions as the Prosecutor claims? Everything in this case testifies to that. The Prosecution even at that point could have offered proof of this visit to the International Red Cross at that point even, but they didn't. The Samac committee, through the evidence invoked by the Prosecution and by the Defence, acted in keeping with instructions by the International Red Cross, although these instructions, as we have seen, were issued in spring 1993. What most worried the Prosecution during the trial is the fact that all the negative occurrences referred to in the report by the Special Rapporteur emphasising the lack of free will and the exercise of free choice, the use of coercion and the impossibility to exercise their rights, this has nothing to do with the work of the commission for the exchanges in Samac. Your Honours, have you ever heard during this trial that someone made anyone else to force a statement that they did not wish it to return? Did anyone chase a person across a minefield during an exchange? Did anyone disappear while being exchanged? Was anyone killed while being exchanged? Was there an exchange on the line of fire, in the line of confrontation, except the one that took place on the 26th of May, 1992, in Zasavica? Were the citizens made to produce any proof that they had complied with their duties? All of this did take place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to the report by the Special Rapporteur, but he does not ever refer to Samac. During this trial, we never had a shred of evidence to this effect. Those were the so-called exchanges, whereas these were exchanges that were carried out in keeping with the rules of the International Red Cross. Did the Special Rapporteur ever refer to Samac, Odzak, or Gradacac or the members of the local commissions? The towns in which Serbs, Muslims and Croats alike, members of the civilian commissions and military commissions worked on a selfless task with a lot of self-sacrifice and all were working in the same manner and along the same -- and on the same principles. That's what all these documents -- documents in this case are talking about. That's what we addressed in our opening argument and all these people speak about Miroslav Tadic. The Prosecutor is placing all of these people in the same position as Miroslav Tadic. The Prosecution wishes to say that such exchanges in their formal definition of ethnic separation by the use of force, that such exchanges were supposed to be a vehicle of ethnic cleansing. If it were up to the Prosecution, they would like to forbid anyone to leave their homes during war in order to keep people from calling this an exercise in ethnic cleansing. That must by all means be prevented. But the word that those people actually carried out would not only be valid by the Prosecution. Where are the people who worked on the exchanges according to the same principles that Miroslav Tadic applied? Safet Kikic, you have him on the recording. He is a public prosecutor, a representative for the Muslim commission. Mijo Matanovic, another person to be shown on the recording. He is the president of the canton assembly of the regional assembly. Grujicic writes books, if anyone cares to read them, and he says in his books wherever they were people who were detained or who had been killed, members of the commission were there too. Amor Masovic, then president of the Federation commission, got an award for the humanitarian worker of the year. Ivan Grujic, today's president of the Croatian commission for missing persons, worked on the exchanges back then, and he still is working on the same tasks. Rodoljub Trkulja, who is referred to in the document of the 1st Krajina Corps, a minister in the government of Republika Srpska. However, the Prosecution thought of Miroslav Tadic of all people, who worked according to the same set of principles as all the other people during the exchanges, all the other people that I've referred to, in order to use him to prove their allegation about the exchanges as a vehicle for persecution. And this is what is so absurd about the accusations related to these exchanges and about the participation in them. The Prosecution cites the example of the exchange that took place on the 4th of September, 1992, and Miroslav Tadic, allowing the women, children, and elderly people who the Prosecutor claims are civilians, and they were, to board the buses on the playground outside the school building. They were followed all the way to Dragalici, and he was responsible, allegedly, because in Dragalic, before the representatives of the International Red Cross, he made it possible for them to say whether they wished to go or to say. He is to blame, they say that Snjezana and Dragan Delic with their two children had to sit on the bus and remain there, and he is to blame that Mladen Borbeli said to the representatives of the International Red Cross that he did not wish to go. Just a note to the interpreters. I am now moving on to page 37, the last passage in that page. The Prosecution is fully aware that the existence of real choice of freedom of choice as to if someone wanted to leave or to stay is the key to the issue of deportation or forced resettlement. That's why I address this question in my final brief. The Defence claims that the choice was there and it was real. It was an option that was offered and it was not a threat or a menace. The fact is that at the time when the persons were making their choice as to whether they wished to stay, leave the prison and cross over to the other side or return to their homes was a real choice that they were given. This is something the Trial Chamber must judge in a truthful light and according to objective criteria. I will now speak again about something that I spoke in our final brief, and this is something that's also common in the fourth Geneva Convention provided by its very creators. The conference especially had in mind the protection of persons belonging to ethnic or political minorities and subject to discrimination or persecution, and therefore perhaps wishing to leave the country. In order to make it possible for them to exercise this legitimate desire, the conference has decided to implicitly approve voluntary resettlement and to only ban forced resettlement or settlement by force. The whole key of this trial, referring to these changes, is whether those who took part in the exchanges through the commission for the exchanges were legitimately exercising their right or desire to leave the area. The motives were plenty: Fear of war, reuniting families, even the desire to fight for the opposite side, of course. But it was made possible for all of them to exercise their legitimate desire and right to choose whether they would stay or leave. Can we please run, briefly, the video, P33, which I have prepared for the Honourable Trial Chamber. I've also prepared a transcript of this interview so the Trial Chamber can follow the video. You have this in the documents. I've also provided a copy for the interpreters. The document is 103A/3. Your Honours, you will hear two brief excerpts from statements provided by persons who were exchanged, a Serb woman and a Croat prisoner.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "My son moved to Belgrade in 1975 and he is working in the Military Medical Academy, and his wife, my daughter-in-law, and his son is working with the army as well. "Inaudible. "It's four years now since my husband died, and I am all alone. "You have nobody. "No, nobody, just me. The children are living on their own, one in Bosnia, and the other in Belgrade. "Inaudible. Two daughters and all my family. "What was your life like in Croatia up to now? "As far as I'm concerned it's okay, but you see, son, what shall I do if I get sick tomorrow, I have nobody to support me and my children are not allowed to come. If I kick the bucket, nobody will dare to come. Now I have applied for the exchange. I will go and join my children. What else can I do?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the other interview, now, please. Can we run the other video now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "So I can hardly complain. "And tell me also where are you intending to go now? "I want to find my family. I have received a message from the Red Cross that the family is in Osijek. So my primary concern is to find my family. As to other things, I don't know. "And then you will probably take a gun again. "I cannot say. This is something I do not decide about. "And would you like that this war comes to an end and the killing stop. "I would by all means like all these evens to stop and that I never have to take the gun again in my hands."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard this from the Prosecution day before yesterday. The Exchange Commissions were separating families. The name of this woman is Danica Blagojevic. Her name was very difficult to make out. Her name might as well have been Marija or Mirsada. She could have been a Croat. She could have been a Muslim. She said: "if I kick the bucket, there is no one to come and see me." And the young man who was released from prison, you will see the whole transcript. Even now the Defence points out, while remaining in their position from the final brief, is that the exchanges that took place through the Samac commission were humanitarian work and all those who wished to leave could exercise their right to leave in a safe and legal way. If the Prosecution is unable to accept the fact that Defence witnesses who talked about Tadic kept using the word "humanitarian" and the Prosecution in their cynicism quoted this in inverted commas. May I remind them then what one of their own key witnesses said of Tadic, page 11696, "I want to greet him on this occasion." The only Prosecution witness greeting one of the accused. Page 11746. [In English] "I greeted him" -- [Interpretation] "I greeted him sincerely because in that" -- [In English] "some humaneness towards me."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Gratitude to him and I can report that again because of his humaneness towards me." All those present in the courtroom know full well who was the man who stated this. When I look at his words, I think he's the most reliable character witness for Miroslav Tadic. This witness, in relation to his own profession, can he be viewed as incompetent to judge someone's humanity or someone's humaneness? I'll leave this up to the Prosecution are. Let them be the judge of this. You know who the witness was who stated this. I must talk about sentencing now, and I must say several words about the Prosecution's sentencing recommendation. They say that the most incriminating circumstance is the voluntary factor with the accused in taking part in the persecutions as well as in the period in which they all carried out the actions as charged. But one cannot prove in the case of Markla [phoen] the mens rea, which is a necessary element of the act. An act does not exist without voluntary action involved which means that it cannot be taken as an aggravating circumstance. If you look at the period relevant to the indictment, then you must draw particular attention to the period in which the person was occupying a certain position, the person indicted was occupying a certain position. The period relative to the indictment is long and we must accused involved in the separate periods during this whole period relevant to the indictment. The Prosecution claims that Miroslav Tadic was a key member of the Crisis Staff. The evidence says differently. He became a member of the Crisis Staff on the 23rd of April, 1992, and prior to that he had nothing to do with any authorities or politics. He remained a member of the Crisis Staff until July 1992, and when the War Presidency came into existence, he ceased being a member. Even during that period, he did not come to the meetings very often, and he did not attend a single meeting that the Prosecution refers to as crucial, the one concerning Djurdjevic's appointment or the meeting with representatives of the military authorities concerning a signing of the document of the 13th signatories. The Prosecution's view on the lack of cooperation was addressed by the Defence in our final brief. Here we shall speak about the degree of cooperation necessary for cooperating with the Tribunal, which is what they said the other day. This is not in the Rules. The Rules only speak about cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor. And this is the kind of cooperation that we addressed in our final brief. Cooperation with the Tribunal, in our view, can only be related to assisting the Court and the economic nature of the trial itself, and that is what Tadic testified to, if you just think back to that. The admission of that is very essential as concerns cooperation with the Tribunal, but what the Rules actually state is cooperation with the Prosecutor. As for what the Prosecutor claims in his final brief and in the closing arguments, they did nothing but admit that Tadic's cooperation was significant and considerable, because they do refer to his cooperation and to the interviews which he granted them. Both the quality and the quantity of this cooperation were essential and considerable. They keep referring to that and they keep quoting Tadic in that respect. The fact that he surrendered only 16 months after the indictment was published, we shall not speak about that, because the Trial Chamber has already evaluated these facts in their judgement of Milan Simic. They both surrendered on two consecutive days. But for the sake of the transcript, we wish to state the following: Miroslav Tadic, I'm deeply convinced, was the first accused to actually phone the Prosecutor and to agree to be interviewed by phone. Now, am I correct in stating this? I don't know. I'm not seeking an answer from the Prosecution, but what I would like to ask them to do is to look again at their views when they state that he offered no cooperation whatsoever. I will just say a couple of words concerning Tadic's character. This goes I think to his mens rea, and I did address this in my final brief, but I must say something for the sake of myself and for the sake of Mr. Tadic now. I've spent years sitting with him in the Detention Unit working on this case, speaking about the tragedy that he went through after the death of his parents. He never referred to this. He never even told me. It was some other people who told me. When I asked him if he wished to refer this to the Trial Chamber, I was aware of the effect that this might have with the Judges and with the Prosecution. He didn't give me an answer. I was aware that the whole story of his family, of him socialising with Croats, would show him as a highly moral person, and I saw his reaction after he was asked the question by Judge Williams. And it was then that together with Tadic I understood in this courtroom that he proved to be exactly the man that I believed him to be, and that's why he's fully entitled to say, proudly so, that 40 members of his family, different members of his family, are in mixed marriages, that his daughter was married to a Croat, that he has two grandchildren from that marriage and that he was friends with Vinko Dragic's grandfather, who was an Ustasha. How come then the Prosecution numbered several Croats and Muslims who were held by Tadic during the war cynically forgetting the number of those who had been expelled? I will use technical numbers; 31 Croats and Muslims testifying for the Prosecution. They testified against all of the accused. I said 31. They testified against the four accused. 12 Muslims and Croats testified for Miroslav Tadic, out of which -- which were not great friends with him before the war, as you have heard. Some of them were just acquaintances. And I, as Defence counsel, considered it an honour that they agreed to come here and testify before this Trial Chamber. Five of them, I think, spent time in a camp. Are these isolated individual cases with which Tadic -- or against whom Tadic concealed his joint criminal enterprise? Would the help provided to Salkic considered his son's concealment be considered something to support this? He also helped Arslanovic when his wife's funeral had to be organised, he also brought personal belongings to Krajnovic, Mihalj, he gave wood to a Muslim, old Muslim lady, wood from the warehouse of the civilian protection staff. I will now bring my closing arguments to a close, and I will just say a few words concerning the sentence proposed by the Prosecution. The Prosecution basically proposed a life sentence for Miroslav Tadic. Yes, you have heard me well. Perhaps they did not wish to explicitly say so, that in their opinion, Miroslav Tadic could, at the age of 87, fit completely in his environment upon his release from prison. Perhaps they counted on him behaving himself well in prison and therefore being released at the age of 80. Perhaps they believed that his poor health would improve in prison and that this would fulfil the objective of sentencing. When according to what Prosecution proposed, Miroslav Tadic leaves the prison, Stevan Todorovic, somebody who repented before this Court, would already be free for 15 years, fully rehabilitated and socialising with Muslims and Croats. In this way, the international community would protect itself from those people who wanted to help somebody; however, this was seen by someone as being a crime. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Zaric is aware of the fact that before us, the Defence of Mr. Blagoje Simic and that of Mr. Miroslav Tadic gave their closing arguments. Much has been stated in their closing arguments of those things that the Defence of Mr. Zaric wanted to point out as well, in view of the fact that we fully support the position of the Defence of Mr. Simic and Mr. Tadic when it comes to the legal analysis of the jurisprudence of the joint criminal enterprise, we therefore support what has been stated by the other Defence counsel. The Defence of Mr. Zaric stands by what has been stated in our final brief, and during our closing arguments, we will devote most of our attention to responding to Prosecutor's final brief and their closing arguments. Further on, the Defence of Mr. Zaric believes that all of the facts stated in our opening speech were proven by us before this Trial Chamber by way of bringing a large number of witnesses who testified as Defence witnesses for Mr. Zaric. The Defence of Mr. Zaric further considers that the existence of joint criminal enterprise has not been proven beyond reasonable doubt during the trial, especially not at the level of Bosanski Samac municipality. However, even if the Trial Chamber accepts that there was a joint criminal enterprise, even if the Chamber believes that it has been proven, then Simo Zaric definitely was not the person who participated in that kind of enterprise in any way. Even though we support the positions taken by the Defence of Mr. Simic and Mr. Tadic, the Defence of Mr. Zaric believes it necessary to point out some of the aspects contained in the definition of the joint criminal enterprise in accordance with the accepted jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Based on the definition that this Tribunal gave to the joint criminal enterprise in the appeals judgement in Tadic case, which is something that the Prosecution also referred to, both in their final brief and in their closing arguments, it is clear that joint criminal enterprise could be split into three groups, and that mens rea of participants differs based on which group we are talking about. The first group of joint criminal enterprise is the one in which participants act in accordance with the joint goal and where participants have the same kind of criminal intent. The other group is composed of those cases in which participants are personally aware of the fact that there exists a system of abuse and where participants intend to contribute to the joint system of abuse. The third group is composed of those cases where there is a joint intent to follow a certain type of conduct but where an act was committed which, although it falls outside of the criminal intent, still represents a natural and foreseeable consequence of that joint goal. This position reflects two main characteristics of the ways one can participate in committing a crime against humanity, which is a state of mind or awareness on joint acting within an existing agreement, as well as participation in the perpetration of an act which is either included in the agreement or stems from it. Acting within the joint criminal enterprise of an aider and abettor means that they were knowingly assisting or encouraging the perpetrator with intention to contribute to the implementation of an agreed goal. In order for there to be a criminal liability, it is necessary to establish that the accused, in a significant way, participated in implementing the criminal enterprise or that he held a position of authority such that one can assume that he wielded influence over the implementation of the criminal plan and design. In view of the facts established in this case, there are no elements which, according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, are necessary in order to establish that somebody belonged to the joint criminal enterprise. There are no such elements on the side of Mr. Zaric. So either when it comes to participating or when it comes to aiding and abetting. First of all, there was not a scrap of evidence given by the Prosecution that established a state of mind of Mr. Zaric when it comes to existence of a criminal enterprise or when it comes to an intention or willingness on his behalf to contribute or aid to the implementation of the goals of a criminal enterprise. The Defence has proven that Mr. Zaric, from the 5th of January, 1992 and onwards, during the time covered by the indictment, was a member first of the Yugoslav People's Army, and then following that, the Army of Republika Srpska. Similar to all other citizens of the then SFRY in Bosnia and Herzegovina who responded to the mobilisation call-up, so similar to them, Mr. Zaric, as a reserve military commander with a status of non-commissioned officer and a rank of sergeant, became a member of the JNA. As such, he was appointed assistant commander in the 4th Detachment for intelligence and security affairs, morale, and information. Tens of thousands of people who responded to the mobilisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina surely could not have all been aware of the alleged participation in joint criminal enterprise, nor can they be considered as part of that enterprise. By joining the Yugoslav People's Army, Mr. Zaric can certainly not be considered as a person who was aware of -- or the person who intended and was willing to participate in any way in a joint criminal enterprise. Based on the ethnic composition of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army, where Mr. Zaric was assistant commander, and where members of all ethnic communities served who lived in Bosanski Samac, the town, it is clear that members of that detachment cannot be considered part of joint criminal enterprise and who participated in persecution of non-Serb population. The many Muslims and Croats, as well as members of other non-Serb ethnic groups who belonged to the 4th Detachment, was something that was not challenged by the evidence presented before this Trial Chamber. The mere fact that all members of the detachment, regardless of their ethnic or religious background, received military equipment and weapons, clearly indicates that during the establishment and the existence of the detachment, there was no willingness or intention on their behalf to be members of the joint criminal enterprise intended to persecute non-Serbs. Simo Zaric, as well as other members of the 4th Detachment, were never aware of the fact that they were jointly acting within some existing agreement or participating in acts which are covered by that agreement or stem from them and are all part of joint criminal enterprise. Similarly, they were not aware that they acted as aiders and abettors in the joint criminal enterprise, nor did they give knowingly any assistance or encouragement to perpetrators with the intention to contribute to the implementation of an agreed goal. Neither Simo Zaric nor other members of the 4th Detachment had awareness on existence of any plan intended to persecute non-Serb population in town and Bosanski Samac municipality. The final brief of the Prosecution, paragraph 67, states that Simo Zaric had a vital position in the 4th Detachment as assistant commander for intelligence and security, morale, and information and also that he was entrusted to supervise the disarming of the non-Serb population, and that in this way he took part in the forcible takeover of power, knowing that this was being done on the basis of joint criminal enterprise, aimed at persecuting non-Serbs. As for the position of Mr. Zaric in the 4th Detachment and his powers as assistant commander, this was extensively referred to in the Defence final brief. The only thing that the Defence wishes to add to this is something that was never contested before this Tribunal, and that is that the collection of weapons had been ordered by the commander of the 17th Tactical Group to the commander of the 4th Detachment, who further on issued orders to his deputy and his assistant commanders and other soldiers. As for the order he had received, Mr. Zaric had to carry it out, according to all rules of service in the JNA, because if he were to refuse to carry out an order, he would be criminally liable before the competent military organs. All the activities related to this order and carried out by Mr. Zaric consisted of the following: Checking out the way how the order of the commander of the 4th Detachment was being carried out. The members of the 4th Detachment collected weapons only in the Fourth Quarter, which is along the outskirts of town, on the embankments, towards the Bosna and Sava Rivers, where the already deployed members of the 4th Detachment were at their positions. Weapons were collected from all citizens, irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. The goal of that operation was not the takeover of power or the persecution of the non-Serb population, but the safety and security of the members of the detachment, who were already at their positions, in order to prevent them from being in the midst of crossfire. That means that they would not be shot at from the back and from the directions of the Sava and Bosna Rivers. In paragraph 68, the Prosecutor states that the Crisis Staff entrusted Mr. Zaric with the confidential position of head of national security, to which he was appointed less than two weeks after the takeover of power. On the basis of agreement between the civilian authorities and the military, he allegedly had free access to the Territorial Defence building and the SUP, with a view to interrogating non-Serbs who had been detained, beaten, and mistreated on the basis of joint criminal enterprise. According to the position upheld by the Prosecution, the interrogation of prisoners was one of the indispensable acts in promoting the system of persecution. The Prosecutor also states that Zaric's position made it possible for him to transfer about 50 non-Serb detainees to military detention, where their humiliation, mistreatment, and interrogation were continued. These facts were also extensively referred to in the final brief of Mr. Zaric's defence, in paragraphs 70 through 77, and this Defence fully abides by everything it said in that brief. Nevertheless, the Defence deems it necessary to put certain events in chronological order in order to create a truthful picture regarding the activities of Mr. Zaric in the initial days of the conflict. The decision to appoint Mr. Zaric as head of national security was adopted on the 29th of April, 1992. This is document P81. By that date, Mr. Zaric had already carried out the interviews he had with four detainees, namely, Mr. Tihic, on the 20th of April, 1992; and the Bicic brothers; and Omer Nalic, on the 27th of April, 1992. So, after having interviewed these persons, or rather, when he interviewed these persons, Mr. Zaric had not even formally been appointed to the position of head of national security for the municipality of Bosanski Samac. After his formal appointment to this position of head for national security in Bosanski Samac, Mr. Zaric did not carry out a single interview with any one of the detainees. Not a shred of evidence was provided to support that. The Prosecution's allegations regarding the free access that Mr. Zaric had to the Territorial Defence building are unfounded, because, except for the occasion when detainees were being transferred from the Territorial Defence to the barracks in Brcko, Mr. Zaric never entered the Territorial Defence building, and not a single witness who testified before this Tribunal established that he or she had seen Mr. Zaric at the Territorial Defence building. As for the actual interviews, Mr. Zaric carried out these interviews and took these statements on the basis of the orders he had received from his superior officers. Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, commander of the 17th Tactical Group, and the head for intelligence and security affairs in the 17th Tactical Group, Maksim Simeunovic. The objective of taking statements was to establish the involvement of officers of the Yugoslav People's Army from the 17th Tactical Group in the illegal selling of military weapons. This was testified to by witness Nikolic on the following pages: 19306 through to 19317, and Mr. Simeunovic on page 18596 of the transcript. It is precisely for that reason, namely, because he received an order with a clear objective to collect information, Mr. Zaric conducted four interviews only. He conducted four interviews within a time period of ten days. So the interviews and the statements that Mr. Zaric compiled on that basis did not have a discriminatory nature, which must necessarily be established in order to state that persecution was committed, and they were not aimed at persecuting the non-Serb population within joint criminal enterprise. Rather, the objective was to establish the responsibility of the members of the Yugoslav People's Army in the illegal selling of military weapons. What is also unfounded is the claim made by the Prosecution that the position of Mr. Zaric made it possible for him to transfer detainees from the Territorial Defence to the barracks in Brcko. Since the Prosecution did not precisely state which position they specifically have in mind, the Defence is going to deal with two possible options. If the Prosecutor meant the formal position of head of national security held by Mr. Zaric, the Defence wishes to highlight that the transfer of detainees to Brcko was carried out on the 26th of April, 1992, that is to say, before his formal appointment as head of national security. Elementary logic indicates that Mr. Zaric could not have taken advantage of the position that he had not even been appointed to. However, if the Prosecutor meant the position of Mr. Zaric as assistant commander of the 4th Detachment, that position of Mr. Zaric's was not nearly such that he could have independently transferred any detainee from the Territorial Defence to the barracks in Brcko. During the proceedings, it was proven that Mr. Zaric had only initiated the transfer of detainees from the Territorial Defence building to the barracks in Brcko, while the decision about this and the organisation of this transfer were carried out by his superior officers, certainly with his participation. In the final brief of the Prosecutor, in paragraph 69, it is stated that military and civilian authorities entrusted Mr. Zaric with participation in a television interview soon after the takeover of power in which the new Serb authorities continued to humiliate the detained and beaten political adversaries, using them for propaganda purposes, and that Mr. Zaric, aware of their detention conditions, on the basis of joint criminal enterprise, voluntarily took part in the implementation of that task. The evidence presented shows how unfounded such allegations made by the Prosecution are. First of all, the question of voluntary participation in the interview that was given to a journalist from TV Novi Sad was refuted by the statement made by witness Stevan Nikolic, commander of the 17th Tactical Brigade of the JNA, who, before -- who testified before this Trial Chamber that he himself issued an order to Mr. Zaric to give this interview to the journalist from TV Novi Sad. The actual place where he would give the interview was not decided upon by Mr. Zaric himself. It was the journalist from TV Novi Sad who decided about that. Mr. Zaric did not know who all the persons participating in this would be, or whether anybody would be giving an interview at the same time. Relationships of superiority and subordination in military structures do not allow for the possibility for the subordinate not to carry out an order. That was the position of Mr. Zaric. Not a single piece of evidence has been proven that Mr. Zaric received any instructions from the civilian authorities to the effect that he should have given this interview, and the Prosecution did not present any evidence to this effect. Finally, Mr. Zaric could not have known or even assumed what the programme would eventually look like. Mr. Zaric could not have influenced the way the programme would have turned out in any way. Mr. Zaric could not have influenced the fact that his interview might have been used for propaganda purposes, especially bearing in mind the fact that this was a TV programme, a TV station, from Yugoslavia. Mr. Zaric only saw the programme, the final product, when all other viewers saw it, throughout the territory of Yugoslavia. This clearly indicates that there is no willingness, awareness, or intent on the part of Mr. Zaric to participate in a joint criminal enterprise aimed at any kind of persecution. In paragraph 70 of the Prosecutor's final brief, it is stated that Mr. Zaric, acting in his capacity as head of national security, accompanied the Crisis Staff on their visit to Belgrade in late May or early June 1992, on which occasion they met Frenki Simatovic. Something that has not been proven in any way as regards this allegation by the Prosecution is Mr. Zaric's position in capacity as head of national security at the time the visit to Belgrade was made. Aside from the fact that Mr. Zaric never assumed this position, the very decision on his appointment was formally put out of force before the trip to Belgrade. In paragraph 71 of the Prosecutor's final brief, it is stated that in May 1992, the Crisis Staff entrusted Zaric with negotiations surrounding the release of Serbs that had been illegally detained in Odzak, the release of these detainees through an exchange, and that in July 1992, he was appointed deputy president of the war council for security issues in Odzak. By virtue of this position, he was receiving orders and sending reports to the Crisis Staff, which continued the persecution through the use of coercion, forced labour, and looting in Odzak. As far as the Defence is aware, not a single piece of evidence during this trial corroborated the Prosecution's allegation that the Crisis Staff had entrusted Mr. Zaric with negotiations surrounding the exchanges with the Odzak side. The Defence has already thoroughly analysed two contacts of Mr. Zaric with the representatives from Odzak in paragraphs 411 through 420. We do not wish to reiterate this, but we would like to point out the fact that the first contact Mr. Zaric ever made with the Odzak side had been initiated by the Odzak side, and that the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Samac had nothing whatsoever to do with that. The only connection there was the fact that Mr. Zaric had applied for permission to have Witness Q brought out of detention to attend the negotiations. The reason that Mr. Zaric required the presence of Witness Q when he met with the Odzak side was that when he was informed and invited, the Odzak side asked, in as far as it was possible, to bring Witness Q. [Microphone not activated] In the transcript page 81, line 21, when he talked with the other side he only says when he met. Because there was not any meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During those contacts with the Odzak side, Mr. Zaric never negotiated the possibility to carry out an exchange. The Defence has called a number of witnesses to testify to this. Allow me to mention the following witnesses: Kosta Simic, the page in the transcript is 16956; Teodor Tutnjevic, pages 16950 and 16951; and Mr. Ivan Cukic. His deposition, page 7. As for his appointment and the tasks that Mr. Zaric carried out in Odzak, the Defence has addressed this thoroughly in its final brief in paragraph 78 through 84. The only thing we would like to point out yet again is that Mr. Zaric did not receive orders from the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac or report in any way to the Crisis Staff. The Prosecution has not produced a single shred of evidence to corroborate this allegation. The tasks carried out by Mr. Zaric in Odzak had nothing to do with the use of forced labour or looting in Odzak. Throughout this period, throughout this whole month that Mr. Zaric spent in the territory of Odzak municipality, he was a regular member of the Army of Republika Srpska and he worked on collecting information and discovering crimes and criminals, crimes that had been perpetrated against Serbs in Odzak during the time that the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, was in power there. In addition to Mr. Zaric himself, Witness Teodor Tutnjevic, Witness Dusan Gavric, and a Rule 92 witness, Misko Pavic, also testified to this. Furthermore, although in paragraph 72 of their final brief the Prosecutor claims that the participation of Mr. Zaric in the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise is less considerable than the participation of Mr. Simic and Mr. Tadic, the Prosecution nevertheless claims that he had the intent to participate and accepted the intent of persecution. The Defence believes that we have proven that Mr. Zaric in no way participated in the joint criminal enterprise. He never expressed any intent to participate. He never expressed his consent with the goals of this enterprise, this enterprise of persecution, nor did he ever agree with those goals or accept them as his own. However, the Defence of Mr. Zaric fully agrees with the position of the Prosecution, as set out in paragraph 94 of their final brief, that the crime of persecution contains in itself an element of discriminatory intent and that the perpetrator must consciously act or omit to act with the intent to discriminate on racial, religious, or political grounds. In addition to other subjective elements, and in relation to discriminatory intent, the following question must be asked, the question of the significance of motive for criminal law. The Defence is well aware of the fact that the motive is not part of the description of this criminal offence, according to the Statute of the Tribunal, but we believe it is important to raise this issue before this Trial Chamber. The motive is most usually defined as the psychic driving force of a certain form of human behaviour, as the internal driving force which, without the man always being aware of it, drives an individual to certain forms of behaviour. The motive is usually in correlation with the intent and the goal that one wishes to attain. As the act under Article 5(H) of the Statute requires inhumane treatment of civilian -- of the civilian population to be carried out on the grounds of their racial, political, or religious allegiance, consequently, the motives for the perpetration of this act can be different, motives such as hatred, revenge, religious and national intolerance, and the like. It is in our view justified to ask the following question: If the crime of persecution has been committed, is it necessary to establish the motives why the crime of persecution was committed? When we are looking for a specific intent in an act or in a crime, as is the case with the crime of persecution, and this intent must be of a discriminatory nature, then it appears almost indispensable to establish the motives for this action. During the trial, the Prosecutor never proved a single motive on the part of Mr. Zaric that would have acted as the driving force in the creation of discriminatory intent against the non-Serb population. On the contrary; the personal and family circumstances of Mr. Zaric clearly indicate that he could not have had any possible motive for racial, religious, or political discrimination, and he still does not have any such motive. In our view, our view as the Defence of Mr. Zaric, the absence of motive rules out the existence of discriminatory intent, the discriminatory intent being a requisite element for the crime of persecution under Article 5(H) of the Statute. Mr. Zaric's Defence believes it necessary to briefly address another legal issue, which is related to the possibility of the cumulative relationship between the crime of persecution and deportation and unlawful resettlement. Without wishing to discuss the right of the Prosecutor to challenge the right of the Prosecutor to have cumulative charges for both of these crimes set out in the indictment, the Defence prefers to focus on the possibility to prove responsibility and to pronounce a single judgement, a unified judgement, for both these crimes. As for criminal responsibility entailed in international crimes, an issue that is particularly important is the following: Can there be cumulative charges or, in other words, concurrence of crimes, if the actions of an individual display the characteristics of a number of different crimes? Or, on the other hand, are we then dealing with a single crime in some form of a quasi-concurrence? We're trying to give an answer to this question. We should start from the basic nature of international crimes and the way in which they differ from other crimes. That, first of all, means that these crimes, as a rule, are not aimed against an individual, against an individually identified specific person, but are rather committed against an unspecified number of people who are not individually identified. A plan precedes perpetration of international crimes. They also need to be organised in order to be carried out, and they do not represent spontaneous, unruly behaviour of individuals. International crimes are committed continuously and successively in a shorter or longer period of time. All international crimes are committed with premeditation and with some crimes it is necessary for that premeditation to be of a specific nature, namely, to be dolus specialis. However, certain international crimes have their specific characteristics, although some of their forms are almost identical, because the majority of them are based on Geneva Conventions or other international conventions. So that, for example, a murder is mentioned both in violations of Geneva Conventions, Article 2 of the Statute, genocide, Article 4 of the Statute, and crimes against humanity, which is Article 5 of the Statute. This situation is similar with deportation, torture, and infliction of physical and mental pain and suffering. All of this ought to be paid attention to when deciding problems which can arise with cumulative charging and convictions for these crimes. The crime against humanity was not envisaged as an individual crime, either in international conventions or in criminal legislation of certain states. However, in Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal, it is said that the Tribunal has jurisdiction when it comes to prosecution of perpetrators of crime against humanity which encompasses murders, exterminations, slavery, deportation, arrests, torture, rapes, persecution on political, racial, ethnic, or religious grounds, and other inhumane acts, when these acts are aimed against civilian population and are perpetrated during an armed conflict of international or internal nature. Based on these provisions, it follows that there is no essential difference between majority of crimes against humanity and war crimes against civilian population. All of the above acts are incorporated in Geneva Conventions and the 2nd protocol. Therefore, it could be said that these crimes cannot exist as independent crimes, that the acts needed for this crime to exist, the victim, and the time of perpetration, fully coincide or are fully identical to those of the crime against civilian population. Based on this, we have to conclude that the same act cannot be constituted to represent both a crime against humanity and a crime against civilian population, or rather, that this cannot be a case of ideal concurrence of offences or plurality of offences when it comes to these crimes. Crime against humanity covers several alternatively defined acts. Therefore, commission of several of those acts against the same victim will not represent concurrence of several offences, but rather just one single offence. We have to conclude that there is no plurality of offences either when acts described in Article 5 of the Statute are committed successively against certain civilians because the nature of this crime is such that it necessarily is committed against several or a large number of individuals and through several acts of perpetration. However, we must not forget that the Statute, in Article 2, does not list all forms of crimes against civilian population which are envisioned by Geneva Conventions and additional protocols, but rather classifies some of them as crimes against humanity, such as extermination, slavery, deportation, and so on. With respect to what we have said earlier about the crimes described in the Statute of the Tribunal, we ought to describe their relationship in a bit more detail, especially from the aspect of concurrence or plurality of offences. With respect to that, we shall point out two basic principles which have been generally accepted in the theory of criminal law. Concurrence or plurality of offences exists when a perpetrator with a single or several acts committed has committed something that constitutes two or more individual crimes for which he is tried in the same trial and given a single sentence. There we can classify this into an ideal concurrence of offences, when we have one act and several crimes; and a real concurrence of offences, where we have several acts and several crimes. It has also been widely accepted that when one act fulfills requirements needed for several crimes, the perpetrator is not always held responsible for all of the crimes, but rather just for one. This is a case of the so-called quasi-ideal concurrence of offences, and we can have this situation in four cases. The first case is when the perpetrator commits one act which represents -- which have qualifications of several crimes; however, these crimes are such that one is general and one is specific. So the specific crime is a special form of a general crime. This is such a case when we apply the following rule, which is: "lex specialis derogat legi generalis," or rather, the perpetrator is held responsible only for the specific, special crime. I will repeat: "Lex specialis derogat legi generalis." such a relationship would exist if deportation as crime against humanity would appear only as a special form of a deportation as a crime against civilian population. In that case, the perpetrator would be responsible only for the crime in Article 5 of the Statute and not for the one in Article 2 of the Statute. The other instance of a quasi-ideal concurrence of offences is when the crimes committed are subsidiary to each other, so that one crime is the primary one, a basic one, and the other one is the subsidiary one. And here we apply the rule "lex primaria derogat legi subsidiaria" based on which the perpetrator is held responsible only for the basic primary offence. We would have this kind of a case where -- with respect to the same victim. That victim would be, let's say, arrested or tortured, which is Article 5(E) and (G) of the Statute, and the same victim would be killed, which is Article 5(A) of the Statute, in which case the perpetrator would be responsible only for the murder. We can have a quasi-ideal concurrence of offences when two crimes are committed, one of which consumes the other, because in that case we would use or apply the rule "lex consumes derogat legi consumptae." and therefore the perpetrator would be held only for the -- responsible only for the greater offence. For example, we would have a crime of genocide if members of one ethnic group would be initially persecuted, Article 5(H) of the Statute, and then based on that ethnic background, they would be killed, which is Article 4(A) of the Statute. And finally, quasi-ideal concurrence of offences could exist when we have a situation of alternativity. For example, if for one crime there are several possible acts, it is sufficient to commit just one single act. However, the same crime would exist when several envisioned acts are committed against same victim. For example, if somebody was arrested during an armed conflict and then raped and then killed, then we would have only one single crime, which would be a murder based on Article 5(H)(A) of the Statute.
