utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In conclusion of this analysis, the Defence believes that in the particular case, in this case which is before this Trial Chamber, among deportation, under Article 5(H) of the Statute and the act of unlawful deportation and transfer set forth in Article 2 of the Statute, there is a relationship of a special and general criminal offence, and therefore one person cannot be held responsible for both of these crimes because here we have a case of ideal concurrence of offences. The Defence raised this issue in view of the fact that this theory is a theory of continental law and since we believe this Court to be a mixture of continental law and common law, then, in our opinion, the Trial Chamber should agree with this position, which is something that is supported by us lawyers who come from the continental legal system. The Defence of Mr. Zaric will now turn to individual charges contained in the 5th amended indictment and assertions of the Prosecution regarding that in their final brief. In paragraph 111 of the final brief of the Prosecution, it is stated that the command of the 17th Tactical Group, under coordination with Milos Bogdanovic, sent a group people to attend special training in Ilok, which is in Serbian Krajina in Croatia, and they supported this with a statement of Milos Savic. The Defence believes that the Tribunal should not draw any conclusions on alleged involvement of the 17th Tactical Group in sending people to Ilok solely based on the statement of Milos Savic, in view of the position he held in the 1st Detachment, which is that of an ordinary rank-and-file soldier, as well as that after they returned to Batkusa, he was a member of the Serbian police in municipality of Bosanski Samac, under the command of Stevan Todorovic and civilian authorities. And this is what witness Naser Sejdic said in his evidence, who was himself a member of the Serb police. Taking into account a fairly low position in the hierarchy that this witness held, his knowledge as to who organised the departure of these people to attend training is pure speculation, and in that regard, of much more significance is the testimony of witness Maksim Simeunovic, who was chief of security and intelligence affairs within the 17th Tactical Group, as well as the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Stevan Nikolic, who testified here before this Honourable Chamber and said that they knew nothing about people being sent to attend training in Ilok. In terms of the meeting in Donji Zabar a day after the Specials landed in Batkusa, the Prosecution, in paragraph 114 of their final brief, claimed that then the Specials were placed under the command of the 17th Tactical Group and they say that this is corroborated by the testimony of Stevan Todorovic. As for the testimony of Stevan Todorovic and his credibility, a lot was said about this in the final brief of Mr. Zaric's Defence. The Defence is only pointing out the testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, in relation to the same event. He stated that at the meeting in Donji Zabar that was held on the 12th of April, 1992, the leaders of policemen from Republika Srpska Krajina were present, Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, and Srecko Radovanovic, Debeli, as well as Blagoje Simic, Mirko Jovanovic, president of the Executive Board of the Serb municipality of Samac, and Stevan Todorovic, chief of the Serb police of the Serb municipality of Samac. And that they said to him then that these persons were members of the police. This testimony of witness Nikolic is on transcript pages 18453 to 18456. Also, witness Nikolic stated that these persons who came by helicopter to Batkusa on the 11th of April, 1992 were never under the command of the 17th Tactical Group or within its actual ranks. This is contained in his statement, namely, D47/4. In relation to the claims made by the Prosecution in paragraph 117 regarding the meeting between Blagoje Simic and Nikolic, which purportedly took place on the 15th of April, 1992, the Defence of Mr. Zaric wishes to point out that with the exception of Todorovic, who claimed that he had indirect knowledge about this, neither Blagoje Simic nor Stevan Nikolic corroborated in their testimonies that such a meeting -- that any meeting ever took place on the 15th of April, 1992 between the two of them. The Defence of Mr. Zaric, on this basis, believes that this fact was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt. In paragraph 118, it is stated that on the 17th of April, in the morning, in Crkvina, the members of the Crisis Staff were present, as well as Fadil Topcagic and Dimitrije Ivanovski from the 4th Detachment. Bearing in mind the detailed explanation that Fadil Topcagic gave in his statement according to Rule 92 bis - this is D34/4 - also in his testimony before this Tribunal during his cross-examination by the Prosecution in connection with his coming to Crkvina, the question arises as to this particular specific case and the relevance of the fact therein, that Fadil Topcagic and Dimitrije Ivanovski were members of the 4th Detachment. The Defence believes that this fact is of no relevance in this case. In paragraph 119 of the final brief of the Prosecution it is stated that witness Milos Savic during the night of the 16th of April came to the silo and that he found the members of the 4th Detachment there and also that this was confirmed by the testimony of witness Aleksandar Jankovic. It is possible that these witnesses did come across members of the 4th Detachment by the silo, but they could have only come across the members of the 4th Detachment that were patrolling the outskirts of town, where the mentioned silo is. And also, these patrols were carried out on the basis of the agreement reached between all political structures at the meeting of the council for security at the local commune of Bosanski Samac. As for these patrols, witness Radovan Antic referred to them, commander of the 4th Detachment, then, Jovo Savic, deputy commander of the 4th Detachment, and Mr. Zaric himself. Also that these patrols were part of the regular tours of the outskirts of the town of Bosanski Samac. As for the allegations made by the Prosecution in paragraph 122 that two witnesses of the Prosecution heard Mr. Zaric talking through a Motorola in the early morning hours of the 17th of April, 1992, the Defence has already addressed this in its final brief. The fact that witness Aleksandar "Aco" Jankovic, as a member of the Serb police, had a Motorola precisely testifies to the extent to which members of that unit were equipped. They were so well equipped as opposed to the 4th Detachment, which did not have such means of communication. Not at a single point in time was it controversial in these proceedings that Mr. Zaric during the night between the 16th and 17th of April 1992, was it controversial that Mr. Zaric met Aleksandar Jankovic or had any contact with him. So the only conclusion that can be drawn on the basis of the evidence presented is that during that night, through the Motorola, the witnesses of the Prosecution heard the communications between members of the special Serb police, or rather, the Specials. It would not be -- it could not be upheld if the Trial Chamber were, on the basis of the testimonies of two witnesses, to accept this allegation made by the Prosecution, that Mr. Zaric, on that morning of the 16th and 17th of April, talked over a Motorola, especially bearing in mind that a voice is distorted through radio communications. As for the collection of illegal military weapons from the citizens of Bosanski Samac, there has been sufficient reference made to that, both in the briefs of the defences of Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic, as well as in the closing arguments, and therefore the Defence will no longer speak about these allegations made by the Prosecution. The assertion of the Prosecution that the SDS Crisis Staff could not have taken over civilian authority without military assistance, or could not have remained in power without support and participation of the military raises an additional question, and that is: Once the objective of the 4th Detachment and the action taken by them on the 17th of April, 1992, still the preservation of the newly established government or something else. The Defence has proven that the 4th Detachment, through actions related to setting up defence lines and collecting weapons, military weapons, in the Fourth Quarter, carried out legitimate military operations of a defensive nature, on the basis of orders received from a Superior Command. The 4th Detachment did not protect or support the newly established government and Crisis Staff, nor did it take part in the joint criminal enterprise of persecution, as alleged by the Prosecutor. The 4th Detachment defended the citizens of Bosanski Samac from incursions made by the forces of the HVO and the army of the Republic of Croatia from the directions of Prud and the Republic of Croatia, on the basis of orders they had received from the command of the 17th Tactical Group. There was nothing illegal, unlawful, or discriminatory in the orders that the 4th Detachment received and carried out. None of these orders have any characteristics of a crime. The duty of the 4th Detachment and its commander, Radovan Antic, as a JNA unit, as well as of all its members, was to carry out orders issued by their Superior Command, in this specific case, the command of the 17th Tactical Group. And the 4th Detachment did carry out these orders. The question of coordination between the members of the 4th Detachment and the members of the paramilitaries and the police in terms of collecting weapons, and this is something that the Prosecution indicates in paragraph 130, is best refuted by the fact that a certain number of members of the 4th Detachment were arrested by members of the paramilitary and the police, on the 17th of April, 1992, and that weapons were seized from a large number of members of the detachment. Witnesses testified about that. Mihajlo Topolovac, Vaso Antic, Petar Karlovic. Had there been coordination in carrying out the operation of weapons collection between the 4th Detachment and the paramilitaries and the police, as alleged by the Prosecution, it is quite certain that members of the 4th Detachment could not have been arrested or have their weapons taken from them. While commenting Exhibit P127, a document of 13 signatories, the Prosecution, in paragraph 133, draws a fully erroneous conclusion in connection with the following: That Colonel Nikolic recognised the group of Specials as an elite unit of Serb commandos before the forcible takeover. The document itself shows that this was some five or six days after they had come. The date of their arrival is not contested. That's the 11th of April, 1992, when five or six days are added to that date, it is obvious that this is the time immediately upon the forcible takeover of Bosanski Samac, when this group publicly became an integral part of the Serb police of Bosanski Samac. Not a single one of the military documents that the Prosecution refers to in paragraph 134of their brief, and these are documents P19, P21, and P23, indicates that there was any coordination and cooperation between the military and paramilitary forces in respect of the takeover of power in Bosanski Samac. The Prosecutor's remark concerning document D28/4, saying that it's self-incriminating and that it speaks about the 4th Detachment taking over control over vital facilities and buildings in the town is, to say the least, ill-founded. This is an announcement made by the 4th Detachment, dated 19th of April, 1992. First and foremost, this announcement of the 4th Detachment dated 19th of April, 1992, was addressed to Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and Yugoslavs. It was addressed to people belonging to all the different ethnic groups, exhorting them to help the 4th Detachment in its task of defending the town. The announcement was written following an attack by the HVO from the direction of Prud on the 18th of April, 1992, and after the shelling of Samac from the territory of the Republic of Croatia had begun. Speaking of control over the vital facilities and buildings, this announcement makes clear that a military viewpoint is being discussed, namely, the banks of the River Sava, the bridges, and the features suitable for putting up resistance to the attack by the enemy. Whatever the Prosecution thinks about this document, one thing is certain: The announcement as a document by the 4th Detachment does not contain any discriminatory intent whatsoever, and it was not a document meant to incite discrimination on racial, ethnic, or religious grounds. The allegation of the Prosecution in paragraph 136 of the brief that it was not important whether the 4th Detachment actually took part in the takeover from the very beginning of the attack, or rather, joined in in the course of the day on the 17th of April, but that there was a deliberate failure to react to an armed rebellion against duly elected, legally elected government was designed to help the newly created Serb authorities consolidate and pave the way for the joint criminal enterprise. This has already been commented on in our final closing argument. It has not been known to happen up to now that the JNA ever participated in the overthrow of any government, not in the municipalities that were populated by Muslims as the majority group, not in the Croat-dominated municipalities, and not in the Serb-populated municipalities. That, after all, was never the remit of the JNA. We believe that something needs to be added to these two remarks of the Prosecution. The position of Simo Zaric in deciding how the detachment was to be used and what its tasks would be is far above his level of responsibility. Mr. Zaric, as has been proven, had no authority to command. The only people who could actually exercise command over the 17th Tactical Group were commanders Stevan Nikolic; the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Antic; and his deputy, Jovo Savic. This Trial Chamber has had occasion to hear four witnesses, Witness Nikolic, Witness Simeunovic, Witness Antic, and Witness Savic. All these four witnesses were Mr. Zaric's superior officers. All four of these witnesses confirmed before this Trial Chamber that they were the ones issuing orders to Mr. Zaric and that Mr. Zaric carried out those orders. What the Defence of Mr. Zaric would like to know is the following: What was the criterion applied by the Prosecution when indicting Mr. Zaric, bearing in mind the fact that Mr. Zaric had four other persons who were in terms of their authority his superiors and who had the authority to issue orders to him, who did in fact issue orders to him, orders that he was bound to carry out? Reflecting on the testimony of Jovo Savic in paragraph 137, the Prosecution reiterates the allegation from the previous paragraph, about the fact that the operations carried out by the 4th Detachment made possible a consolidation of the newly established authorities in Bosanski Samac. As we have already spoken about this, about the objective of the orders that the 4th Detachment received and carried out, the Defence will no longer address these issues. In paragraph 138, the Prosecution again makes an allegation in reference to the document of the 13 signatories, that Nikolic welcomed the Serb Specials before the takeover of the town. It is our position that we have succeeded in proving that this allegation is false. We would like to point out that the use of the expression "liberation of Bosanski Samac" was common in that time. It was the way people spoke. The term was widely used in all military documents of the time in reference to areas controlled by the Serb forces. This term was also used in reference to areas under the HVO and the BH army. Finally, bearing in mind the allegation of the Prosecution that Mr. Zaric in his interview to the OTP said that Nikolic had placed the paramilitaries under his command, the Defence would like to invite the Trial Chamber to go back to the audio recording of Mr. Zaric's interview to the OTP, Exhibit Number P140 ter, in order to establish once and for all that Mr. Zaric was talking about placing the paramilitaries under the control and not under the command of the 17th Tactical Group, or rather, Commander Nikolic. On the basis of everything we have said, it is clear that the allegation of the Prosecution in paragraph 139 is completely unfounded, namely, their allegation that the JNA and the Serb paramilitary forces were subject to the same command structure of the JNA, both prior and following the takeover, and that they acted together in carrying out the joint criminal enterprise. The allegation made by the Prosecution contained in paragraphs 145 and 146 that members of the 4th Detachment arrested men of Croat and Muslim ethnicity is likewise completely unfounded. The Prosecution refers to Ibrahim Salkic's testimony, a witness who was not at all arrested by Fadil Topcagic, but rather by two persons who took him away in a car to the SUP building and who, in Salkic's own testimony, were not even members of the 4th Detachment. Witness Fadil Topcagic, who testified before this Trial Chamber, stated that a while ago, Ibrahim Salkic came to see him at his home, together with his family, crying and told him that he had lied before the Tribunal in relation to him and Simo Zaric, a testimony that this Trial Chamber has heard before. Furthermore, the testimony of Osman Jasarevic that he was arrested by the members of the paramilitary alongside with Nikica Bjelojevic, of whom Jasarevic said that he was a member of the 4th Detachment of the JNA, is false. It has not been contested that Jasarevic was not a member of the detachment and that he did not know who were the members of the detachment and which persons were not members of the detachment. So his assertion that Bjelojevic was a member of the 4th Detachment is pure speculation. The Prosecution's conjecture in paragraph 150 of their brief that it would not have been logical for the 4th Detachment to start disarming the paramilitary units of the SDA and the HDZ, asking them to hand over their weapons of their own free will, remains merely in the realm of speculation. On the basis of a fact that had been proven, namely, that the 4th Detachment collected weapons in the Fourth Quarter, in which no units of the HDZ and SDA were present or active, unlike the centre of town. It is clear that this allegation of the Prosecution has no foundation in the evidence. In paragraph 153, the Prosecutor, when explaining the reasons for the arrest of certain persons, among other things, invokes witnesses Mustafa Omeranovic and Witness M. First of all, Witness Mustafa Omeranovic spent only one day in detention, after which Commander Nikolic, Lieutenant Colonel commander of the 17th Tactical Group, and alongside with the other detained members of the 4th Detachment, he was released. Witness M was fully familiar with the reasons for his arrest in September 1992, namely, shooting and injuring witness Stevan Arandzic, who himself testified to this in the form of deposition in Belgrade, transcript page 170. The allegation that the -- there was no reason to arrest this witness, the allegation made by the Prosecution, is completely unfounded. In connection with paragraph 154 in the Prosecutor's brief and the alleged participation of Mr. Zaric in the interrogation of Ibrahim Salkic, the Defence of Mr. Zaric wishes to point out that neither the testimony of Ibrahim Salkic himself nor that of any other witness or evidence, can we gather that Mr. Zaric ever interrogated this particular witness, Mr. Salkic. On the contrary, Mr. Zaric briefly entered the office in the SUP building, in which this witness was being interrogated by the chief of the crime department, Milos Savic. Testimony of witness Salkic can be found in the transcript, page 3293 and 3294. The allegations made by the Prosecution in paragraph 160 that Mr. Zaric was conducting interviews together with a journalist are completely unfounded. Exhibit P16 clearly indicates that all questions, those addressed to Mr. Zaric and those addressed to the remaining participants, or rather, persons being interviewed, were asked only by this journalist of the Novi Sad TV, Minja Pavlovic. So that the allegation that Mr. Zaric conducted these interviews together with the journalist is totally unfounded. Much has been said about this interview and therefore the Defence does not wish to repeat our assertions. Now, as regards the allegations in paragraph 164, namely, that Mr. Zaric told Witness Q that he could only be exchanged in the all-for-all exchange, the Defence points out that this fact that Witness Q did not wish to be exchanged until all members of his flock crossed over to the other side, in addition to Mr. Zaric, Witness DW1/3 testified about this as well, in the same way that Mr. Zaric did. Not one of the witnesses, Kosta Simic, Teodor Tutnjevic, Bozo Ninkovic, who were present during the conversation between Witness Q and Father Ivo Simic from Odzak, confirmed allegations of the Prosecution contained in this paragraph. Invoking the testimony of Mr. Zaric in paragraph 165 of their final brief and commenting on the reasons which prompted Mr. Zaric to say to some prisoners that they were political prisoners, the Prosecution knowingly ignored a fact that has been established clearly during the trial, namely, Witness Sulejman Tihic, Witness Dragan Lukac, and Witness A, who were in the group that Mr. Zaric called a group of political prisoners, in their testimony confirmed that they were in possession of illegal firearms, military firearms. Allegations of the Prosecutor that Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric had a significant role in discriminatory arrests, which is described in paragraph 177, is completely unfounded, are completely unfounded. Participation in overseeing collection of weapons is not related to arrests at all, nor could Mr. Zaric at all suppose that there would be arrests after the event of the 17th of April, 1992. Furthermore, Mr. Zaric never used prisoners in propaganda purposes, nor did he participate in negotiations on the exchanges. Neither can the interrogation of several detainees in order to uncover a chain of illegal weapons trade on involvement of members of the JNA may be considered a discriminatory act. What is especially indicative is that when Prosecution, in paragraph 188 of their final brief, in speaking about the massacre in Crkvina, they failed to mention the conduct of Simo Zaric following his finding out that there had been this crime. This is not coincidental, because all of the acts of Mr. Zaric are contrary to all of the claims of the Prosecution about him being a member of the joint criminal enterprise. Public condemnation of this crime which took place in Crkvina informing the superiors, travelling to Belgrade in order to report on the crime. All of this clearly demonstrates that Mr. Zaric did not accept and was, in fact, was opposed to what was going on in Bosanski Samac municipality. Mr. Zaric condemned, in strong terms, this crime, in the document of 13 signatories, which is Exhibit P127, and he did that even before this Tribunal was founded. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber ought to ask itself whether this is a typical conduct of a person who was a member of a joint criminal enterprise and who accepts the goals of that enterprise. In its brief, the Defence devoted significant attention to an event described in paragraph 202 of the Prosecution's final brief and pertains to the testimony of Ibrahim Salkic, about how he saw Mr. Zaric in front of the SUP building with Stoko Sekulic during the visit of the International Red Cross. Salkic himself didn't say that Mr. Zaric entered the premises of the TO, and this testimony can be found on page 3282 and 3283 of the transcript. Neither did witness Stoko Sekulic, who testified that on that occasion, Milan Simic was with him, rather than Mr. Zaric. Witness Sekulic testified about that on page 18065 of the transcript. Therefore, this allegation of the Prosecution remains completely unfounded. The attempt of the Prosecution to depict the transfer of prisoners from the building of the TO to the barracks in Brcko as another proof in favour of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise is simply unbelievable. This can be found in paragraphs 204 to 206. The humane reason for transferring those prisoners is thus distorted and put in a context where they don't belong. Mr. Zaric's position concerning the transfer of prisoners and reasons that led to that is something that can be gleaned from the testimony of Sulejman Tihic, who, when describing that event, said that Simo Zaric joyfully hugged him and kissed him and told him they were saved, after ensuring that they would be transferred from the TO building to the garrison in Brcko. This testimony of Mr. Tihic can be found on page 1445 of the transcript. The Defence would like to ask the Trial Chamber to once again ask itself whether this would be a typical behaviour of a person who willingly participates in joint criminal enterprise and shares its g goals. In paragraph 206, the Prosecution accepted that the conditions in the barracks in Brcko were significantly better than those in the TO building in Bosanski Samac. However, with the proviso that that lasted for a very brief time and that after the conflicts broke out in Brcko, the prisoners were transferred to Bijeljina, where once again they were treated harshly and inhumanely. In addition to what was already stated concerning the position and responsibility of Mr. Zaric in the 4th Detachment, namely, that he neither could decide nor organise the transfer of prisoners, the Defence would simply like to add that the barracks in Brcko is located outside the area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment, whereas the one in Bijeljina, outside of the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group. So that everything that happened to the prisoners was completely outside the scope of responsibility and authority of Mr. Zaric. Allegations of the Prosecution that Fadil Topcagic, as member of the 4th Detachment, returned prisoners from Batajnica to Bosanski Samac, which can be found in paragraph 208 of the Prosecution's brief, is completely -- are completely groundless, because at that time, the 4th Detachment existed no longer, and the circumstances surrounding the travel of Topcagic to Batajnica to bring back prisoners are explained in detail in his 92 bis statement and were not challenged during his cross-examination before this Trial Chamber. Paragraphs 216 to 223 of the Prosecutor's brief contain some similar allegations concerning Mr. Zaric's interview to the Novi Sad television. Not one of the Prosecution's witnesses stated that Zaric forced them to talk to journalists. His participation in the TV Novi Sad interview should be seen in what it actually was, namely, that he was one of participants, he was one of persons giving interview, he came there on orders of his superior and spoke about his knowledge on the paramilitary formations in Bosanski Samac based on documents that had been found and documents that were shown in the footage. The authenticity of those documents was confirmed by witness Alija Fitozovic, as well as numerous other witnesses heard during the trial. I will simply list the following witnesses: Todorovic, Sarkanovic, and Jekic. In paragraph 230, the Prosecution claims, and this is completely unfounded, that members of the 4th Detachment took workers to perform forced labour. Much has been said about the extent of speculations of Prosecution witnesses as to who was and who was not a member of the 4th Detachment. They did not have real, truthful information regarding that, especially during the relevant stated period of time, the Army of Republika Srpska was already established, so that the soldiers were members of the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska, rather than the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army. A large number of people wearing uniforms and having weapons were not members of the 5th Battalion, but rather had various posts within police, Ministry of Defence, and other organs. That is the case of Mile Zoranovic, called Pancir, who most frequently guarded persons performing forced labour and was not a member of the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska. Explaining the participation of the accused and the forced labour, the Prosecution, in paragraph 252, states that Mr. Zaric's wife was forced to sweep streets. This fact precisely shows us what was the influence of Mr. Zaric when it came to work obligation and to what extent he was capable of relieving at least his wife of the duty to sweep streets, regardless of how much he desired to do that. In the same paragraph of the Prosecution brief, they refer to the statement of Witness K, who allegedly was ordered by Mr. Zaric to sweep streets in Odzak, and this is a complete distortion of facts which had been established during the trial. The tasks performed by Mr. Zaric in Odzak had nothing to do with the people performing work obligation. The jobs performed by workers who had work obligation were assigned by commissioners, by the commissioner for the town of Odzak, whose name is Dusan Gavric. Dusan Gavric gave evidence to that effect before this Trial Chamber. As to the testimony of Witness M and his credibility, I will say that that was covered quite well in the final brief. Therefore, we believe it is not necessary to add anything to that. In its brief, the Defence also dealt with the quite unfounded allegations made by the Prosecution in paragraph 253, that Mr. Zaric allegedly freed Snjezana Delic of work obligation. Since this was explained in detail in paragraphs 365 to 367 of the final brief of the Defence, what the Defence wishes to point out now is that Mr. Zaric addressed Milos Bogdanovic, who, as head of the department of the Ministry of Defence, was in charge of questions related to work obligation too, and that what is most likely is that precisely Bogdanovic reacted by drawing the attention of Stojan Blagojevic to the fact that Snjezana Blagojevic, as the mother of two young children, was not subject to work obligation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Snjezana Delic, not Snjezana Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is also unfounded to state that at the request of Snjezana Delic's father-in-law to have her problem heard can be considered to -- can be considered as giving authorisation to free someone of work obligation. There is ample evidence that was heard during these past two years, and no one mentioned that Simo Zaric was in charge of work obligation in the town of Bosanski Samac. Also, what is stated in paragraph 254 of the Prosecutor's brief is unfounded, that Mr. Zaric, as a senior officer in the 4th Detachment was involved in the programme of forced labour, invoking the testimony of Safet Dagovic involving a speech that he allegedly made in August 1992 in front of the memorial centre. Witness Jovo Savic, in his testimony, clearly stated that he was the person who made a speech before the 5th Battalion, and also that Milos Bogdanovic was present then as well, who also made a speech on behalf of the ministry. It is not being challenged that this is a time period when Mr. Zaric had duties in Odzak. So the Prosecutor would have to make up his mind. What are the duties that Mr. Zaric carried out in the month of October 1992? There is just one thing that is certain, and that is that he could not have been in two different places at the same time, both in Samac and in Odzak. Even the testimony of Witness M, in contrast to what witness Dagovic said about this, is in contrast to what witness Dagovic said about this, and therefore this testimony of his cannot be accepted as reliable evidence in these proceedings. Paragraphs 276 to 291 of the Prosecution brief pertain to the specific accusation levelled against Mr. Zaric, namely, taking statements from detained persons. The Defence of Mr. Zaric can only take this to be as a lack of legal arguments and proper evidence in the hands of the Prosecution. As for taking statements from a few detainees by Mr. Zaric, the Defence already stated its views in its final brief, and it will now respond only to some of the assertions made by the Prosecution. The Prosecutor believes that taking statements from detained persons constitutes participation in a system of discriminatory interrogations, with the knowledge that vis-a-vis detained non-Serbs, persecution is being carried out by other participants in the joint criminal enterprise. This thesis is unfounded, as far as Mr. Zaric is concerned, on the basis of the evidence presented here. As for the allegations made by the Prosecution about some kind of a central role played by Mr. Zaric in the interviews, that is totally unfounded, particularly bearing in mind the fact that he interviewed only four detainees. All statements of detainees that were given to Mr. Zaric were compiled truthfully. Nothing was added to them and nothing inaccurate was entered into them. When statements were taken, no force or threats were resorted to on the part of Mr. Zaric, which was confirmed by all witnesses who testified in this regard, namely, Mr. Tihic and the Bicic brothers, Muhamed and Hasan Bicic. We've already said what the objective was of having these statements taken. This had to do with finding out who the JNA officers were, who were involved in illegal weapons sales. When statements that have become part of evidence are quite simply read, and these are exhibits D8/4 and D9/4, it's quite clear that they do not differ in any way from what these witnesses stated before this Tribunal as well. Although other evidence also clearly indicates that these two witnesses, Muhamed and Hasan Bicic, did take part in fighting in Bosanski Samac on the 17th of April, 1992, as well as that Mr. Zaric was aware of this fact, this is not contained in their statements given to Mr. Zaric in Brcko, which, in addition to the other facts that were mentioned, clearly shows that they were not treated in a discriminatory fashion at all. As for the allegations contained in paragraph 284 that Mr. Zaric purportedly ordered the duty policeman to beat Kemal Mehinovic, the Defence claims that Mehinovic's statement is quite untruthful and this was refuted in the best possible way by the evidence that was presented during Mr. Zaric's Defence case. First of all, pictures of the interior of the SUP building from Bosanski Samac, along with the details of the room where Mehinovic was detained as well as the direction in which the door opens shows quite clearly that he could not have seen Mr. Zaric by the entrance, as he claimed before this Tribunal. This video footage of the police station is D44/4. This is what witness Vladimir Sarkanovic testified about as well. His statement can be found in the transcript on page 16548. This witness spent his entire career in the police station in Bosanski Samac, and he confirmed that the door on these particular premises was not changed since 1992, and finally, witness Savo Djurdjevic, page 17631 of the transcript, who was on duty when Kemal Mehinovic was beaten, stated categorically and testified that Simo Zaric had not ordered that, or that he never gave any such orders, nor could have he given such orders to have any of the detainees beaten. In paragraph 286 of the final brief, the Prosecution again is trying to diminish the importance of Zaric's behaviour in term of initiating the transfer of detainees to Brcko, claiming that the reason for this was to continue taking the statements concerned in an unhindered fashion. Such a position taken by the Prosecution has a deficiency in the field of logic and that is that there were no impediments in Mr. Zaric's way to take these statements in Bosanski Samac and also that out of the 56 persons that were transferred to Brcko, only three gave statements. Mr. Zaric was never aware that when taking statements, he was in any way acting in a discriminatory manner or that this in any way constitutes a contribution to joint criminal enterprise in terms of persecution. The Defence underlines yet again that the only objective for having these statements taken, the ones that Mr. Zaric took, that is, was to establish the involvement of officers of the Yugoslav People's Army in illegal sales of military weapons. The Defence of Mr. Zaric believes that the allegations of the Prosecution contained in paragraph 310 of the final brief do not correspond to the evidence adduced, namely, the allegation that early in the month of May, the Crisis Staff asked Mr. Zaric, Mr. Tadic, and Bozo Ninkovic to negotiate about the exchange of prisoners who are being held by Croats in Odzak is quite contradictory to what was said during their testimonies with regard to this event by Bozo Ninkovic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric himself. All three testified that they took part only in compiling lists of Serbs who remained in the territory of the municipality of Odzak, and that they did not conduct any negotiations that had to do with exchanges. Their engagement was over once the lists were compiled and once these lists were handed over to the local Red Cross. Obviously, this activity of Mr. Zaric's, which has nothing to do with exchanges, but the Prosecution, for want of other evidence, is trying to put Mr. Zaric within a context of exchanges, nevertheless. The allegations made in paragraph 321 about Mr. Zaric informing the Crisis Staff about developments in his negotiations with Odzak are exaggerated. Bearing in mind that Mr. Zaric reported to the Crisis Staff only once to the effect that Odzak was proposing an exchange on an all-for-all basis and that after that he did not have any contacts, official or unofficial ones, with the Crisis Staff in respect of the exchanges issue. The allegations contained in paragraph 322 of the Prosecution brief constitute a partial distortion and changing the meaning of the words that were actually uttered by Mr. Zaric, namely, document P142 ter, pages 79 and 80, clearly showed that Simo Zaric was not the person who was supposed to agree to the proposal made by the Odzak side, along with the consent of the Crisis Staff. The essence of the answer that Mr. Zaric gave to the Prosecutors was that he would convey the proposal of the Odzak side to the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac and that he would then convey the answer of the Samac Crisis Staff to Odzak, when they talk again. This is quite clear from the mentioned parts of Mr. Zaric's interview. The allegations of the Prosecution contained in paragraph 321 are totally unfounded, namely, that Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic together negotiated about the first exchanges after the takeover on the 26th of May in Zasavica and on the 5th of July in Lipovac in 1992. First and foremost, no evidence whatsoever was adduced about Mr. Zaric's participation in negotiations concerning the July exchange in Lipovac, which took place on the 4th of July, 1992. This was never adduced during the proceedings. Mr. Zaric explained during his testimony in which capacity he happened to be at that exchange. It is the position of the Defence that mere presence at the exchange by no means signifies participation in the negotiations or its organisation, as the Prosecution has been trying to represent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions, Simo Zaric had contact with the Odzak side over radio link in the presence of Witness Q. However, he did not, as alleged by the Prosecution in paragraph 326, order Witness Q to propose an all-for-all exchange. Quite the contrary; Witness Q never said that Mr. Zaric had asked any such thing of him. The fact is that after the second conversation there was an exchange, and the Prosecution is trying to use this fact to prove that it was the result of Mr. Zaric's involvement, which, however, is quite groundless, because then the question would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apology, Your Honours. I have the same problem as with the closing argument of the Prosecutor. I would like to have line 6 and 7 on page 114 redacted from the transcript. Lines 6 through 9 on page 114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is: Why would Witness Q have been taken two other times to negotiations together with Miroslav Tadic? Also, numerous evidence coming from witnesses that were heard before this Trial Chamber, Bozo Ninkovic, Kosta Simic, Teodor Tutnjevic, and Mr. Zaric himself, indicates how the second conversation between Mr. Zaric and the representatives of Odzak ended. Mr. Zaric was insulted, threatened, and that was the end of the conversation. No agreement was ever reached. And Mr. Zaric never again went to the premises of the communication centre, nor did he have any further contact with the representatives of Odzak municipality. The Defence would particularly like to point out that Witness Q also stated that Mr. Zaric had left and that he had no further knowledge of what happened. So the portion of his statement referred to by the Prosecutor in their brief is mere speculation on his part. The Prosecution's allegation of Mr. Zaric's alleged announcements on the radio in connection with detaining Croats was refuted by the testimonies of Witness Vaso Antic and Witness Pasaga Tihic who both confirmed that Simo Zaric was never present on the premises of Radio Samac nor did he ever address the public on the radio. His interview to Novi Sad TV was broadcast on several occasions, though. Your Honours, perhaps this would be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to wait for the registry assistant to have the page signed for redaction. And while I'm waiting for that, Mr. Pisarevic, you did give 15 minutes to Mr. Pantelic. I wanted to find out whether it's from your main time of three hours or it's from your reply of one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it boils down to more or less the same for me. I have five pages to go. This may take between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's what you have, actually. That's the balance you have for your three hours. So if you continue tomorrow for 15, 20 minutes, then that will be the end of three hours. And then your reply time will be 45 minutes. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And tomorrow we shall sit from 9.00 only up to 12.30 hours and then continue on Friday from 9.00 up to 13.45 hours. It should be 6 to 9, line 6 to line 9, because counsel continued citing the evidence of the same witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have just a few seconds, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have your guidelines and with regard to the -- tomorrow's scheduling. I mean, based on the principle of the equality of arms and fairness of trial, we believe that since the Prosecution will have more than 18 hours for preparation for rebuttal until tomorrow morning at 9.00 and then we shall be in situation to hear them only tomorrow morning, assuming, let's say, 9.15 or 9.30, then one hour of their submission, and obviously the Defence will be in a little bit unfair situation. So what I kindly ask you, in order to consult with my colleagues, which we could -- because this is a joinder case, which topics we could cover. I would kindly ask you for at least two hours' break tomorrow after the Prosecution's submission so that we could be ready -- or even one Defence team to be ready to proceed. Because, you know, comparing to 18 hours and -- I mean, two hours, it's more than fair, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think if you can discuss that with your colleagues after we have risen and then the matter will be communicated through the legal officer to the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber will be able to say how we shall sit tomorrow and Friday. But whatever happens tomorrow, our proceedings will end at 12.30 hours and then we can continue on Friday. We shall rise now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.
